notes.title: Nightly Penitence
notes.content:
Today, we’ll show you the WIP of this [b]quest marker[/b], for which we used this figure drawn in the Codex Borbonicus.

This figure represents the [b]night[/b] as an eye star surrounded by darkness, above two bloody [b]thorns [/b]which represented self-sacrifice and penitence. 

This icon could be interpreted as the blood poured over the heart of the night; namely, the "[i][b]nightly penitence[/b][/i]".

notes.content:

notes.title: NPCs: a boy from the Uxmal community
notes.content:
We are up to date with our game development goals, so we wanted to show you something we have been working on for quite some time.

Bringing the [b]pre-Columbian [/b]world to life is a humongous task, and we are taking special care on the [b]NPCs[/b] the player will interact with. This is why we are constantly getting in touch with regular contemporary Mexicans from different towns and cities, in order to honor their [b]facial features and skin tones[/b] in our game. For a long time, these kinds of features have not been properly recognized in the media, which is why we want to make a difference with this effort.

Today, we want to introduce a boy from the [b]Uxmal community[/b], who granted us permission to capture his looks and recreate them in our game.

What do you think?

notes.title: The Ceiba tree
notes.content:
Greetings, dear [b]Mictecs[/b]!

Today we want to show you this [b]3D rendering[/b] of a monument built by the Secretary of Arts and Culture of Merida, Yucatan, honoring [b]Ceiba[/b], the world tree.

For pre-Columbian societies, the ceiba tree held the [b]universe in place[/b], which was why the gods planted 4 of them on each [b]cardinal point[/b], each of a different color: the black ceiba was west, the white ceiba on the north, the yellow ceiba south and the red on the east.

This way, the trees represented a [b]bridge [/b]between earth, heaven and the underworld, each made up by several levels: 13 for heaven and 9 for the underworld.

So tell us, what do you think of this homage to Merida, Yucatan?

notes.content:
Greetings travelers!

Today we want to show you these three items you will be able to find scattered around the underworld.

First, a [b]pumpkin[/b], an important element of the pre-Columbian society diet, usually toasted or ground before consumption. 

Second, a [b]maize container[/b], the main food of the pre-Columbian diet as well as the most important product of their economy. 

Finally, a [b]jaguar pelt[/b], a symbol of strength and power.

notes.title: Calendar reading: a concept art
notes.content:
What is the [b]meaning of life[/b]? 

The unavoidable question that dives into the [b]uncertainty [/b]of the future; but pre-Columbian civilization had the certainty that the [b]will of the gods[/b] could manifest itself to us through [b]nature[/b]. 

Their worldview marked the time they lived in, and guided the action of every [b]Mexica[/b], forming what we now know as one of the greatest and most impressive cultures of the world.

Today we want to show you some of the [b]art [/b]created by members of the team behind [i]Mictlan[/i], where a child is brought to a sage to have their [b]calendar reading [/b]done. This 260-day calendar kept sacred dates, established harvest cycles, rains and droughts, read dreams, predicted wars and [b]prophesied the future[/b] of each Mecixa.

Are you ready to know what the gods have in store for you?

notes.title: Camazotz
notes.content:
Traveling through [b]Xibalba [/b]is no easy task, especially if you come face to face with the terrible [b]god of bats[/b]. 

With a humanoid aspect and a underworldly aura, he represents [b]death[/b], [b]night [/b]and [b]sacrifice[/b]. 

[b]Camazotz [/b]was worshiped by the ancient Maya and Zapotecs, and they believed he had the power to cure any disease, as well as sever a person's [b]life thread[/b], which joins our souls to our bodies.

The [b]Popol Vuh[/b] describes him as a large beast with fierce claws and jaws, capable of destroying whoever came before him. The stories tell of how one night, the hero twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque arrived at the house of bats, where Camazotz ruled supreme, and on their crossing the darkest cave of his residence, Camazotz decapitated Hunahpu; it would eventually fall to Xbalanque to restore his twin’s head.

Camazotz is associated with [b]heart extraction [/b]sacrifices. He is a lethal creature who came down from the heavens to decapitate the very first humans, and who now rules in the deepest parts of the Earth.

Are you ready to face the terrible Bat of Death?

notes.title: "Cueitl" and "Hornettes"
notes.content:
Today we will show you this concept art on different [b]dresses [/b]and [b]hairstyles [/b]inspired by historical evidence as well as contemporary communities.

The base of the common everyday clothes of pre-Columbian people was a [b]cueitl[/b], a long rectangular cloak held at the waist with a [b]nelpiloni [/b](either a rope or a belt). 
Cueitl could be plain or decorated with lavish shapes depicting flowers and/or elaborate geometric designs.

These hairstyles were also specifically for women. The one we know the most of is one that historians have dubbed as “[b]hornettes[/b]”, which consisted of braiding the hair over the side of the forehead along with colored cotton thread, forming one braid on each side of the head, each ending with a small point on the top.

notes.title: Photogrammetry
notes.content:
Greetings, warriors!

In this special post, we will show you our team getting to work, led by our creative director [b]Guillermo Alarcón[/b]. 

As you already know, one of the graphic techniques used for creating the look and feel of [i]Micltan [/i]is [b]photogrammetry[/b]; with this method, we can capture and measure terrains, structures or people with [b]incredible precision[/b].

Here you can see a photoshoot with members of an [b]indigenous community [/b]that will be used to create hyper-realistic characters. 

[i]Mictlan [/i]is not only inspired by the past, but also by our common heritage.

notes.title: Tonalpohualli
notes.content:
Hello, [i]Mictlan [/i]gang!
Today we will show you this WIP, which depicts a reading of the [b]Tonalpohualli [/b]to children.

During pre-Columbian times, it was believed that a [b]person’s fate[/b] and character were determined by the [b]day of their birth[/b] in the Tonalpohualli, the sacred 260-day calendar. 

An expert reader was summoned for the reading; these people were known as [i][b]Tonalpouhqui[/b][/i], meaning “reader of destinies”. 

For a precise reading, the Tonalpouhqui had to know the exact moment of the [b]child's birth[/b], whether he/she had been born during the day or the night, before or after midnight. This was crucial, as it determined the[b] child’s sign[/b], which assigned them their fate, virtues and weaknesses. 

So... [i]Are you ready to know your own destiny[/i]?

notes.content:
Dear dwellers of [i]Mictlan[/i], we have a [b]special guest [/b]today.

Out of all the terrible and mysterious creatures that haunt the nights of Ancient Mexico, the most terrifying of all was [b]Yohualtepuztli[/b], or "night ax".

notes.content:
Greetings, [i]Mictlan [/i]community!

Today we will show you this WIP, in which you can see the follow-up of the design for the Spanish conquistador [b]María de Estrada[/b]. 
In one of the images, you can see her wearing the equipment of a light cavalry soldier of the XI century, in which you can observe a [b]medieval-style armor[/b], while on the other she wears the buff coat shown on a picture of the Tlaxcala Codex.
María de Estrada was known for her [b]ferocity [/b]and [b]bravery [/b]on the battlefield, as well as for being skilled both with sword and spear, both on foot and on horseback.

María de Estrada will be one of the many [b]historical characters [/b]you will be able to find in [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i]

notes.title: Fancy hairstyle
notes.content:
A constant of the human race, no matter the time and place, is wanting to have[b] fancy haircuts[/b].

In today’s WIP we’ll show you one of the many hairstyles that people during the Pre-Columbian time wore: this specific style is the [b]neaxtlaualli[/b], which consists of braids pointing at the front of the face. This style was used by married women.

In Aztec culture, people wore different hairstyles based on their [b]profession [/b]and [b]social class[/b]. For example, warriors fixed their hair in elaborated styles and with ornaments, and priests wore their hair long. 
Likewise, different hairstyles, much like clothing, could tell from which part of the [b]empire [/b]or from which [b]tribe [/b]you were.

Hi, [i]Mictlan [/i]followers!

Our talented concept artist, [b]Mauricio Pampin[/b], created this WIP for the armor of heavy infantry soldiers.
This set of protective equipment includes a full cuirass and breastplate (protecting the user’s torso), greaves (covering the knees all the way down to the feet) and helm (guarding the head and face).

Infantry troops were known for going on foot and fighting enemies in [b]melee [/b]combat.

notes.title: Huastec
notes.content:
To advance in rank in the army, you have to achieve [b]feats[/b], even if they’re [b]bloody[/b]...

Today, we enthusiastically show you this WIP of a [b]Cuextecatl [/b]warrior, better known as [b]Huastec[/b], as it is portrayed in the Codex Mendoza.
In the chain of command of the Mexica army, just over the [i]tlamanih[/i], there were the Cuaxtecatl warriors, which were soldiers that captured two enemies in battle. 
This rank was introduced in the army after the military campaign against the Huastecs by the [b]Tlatoani Ahuitzotl[/b]. Warriors wore a distinctive [b]uniform[/b], composed of a red suit called [i]lahuitztli[/i], sandals and a conical hat.

notes.title: Cihuacoatl: a concept art
notes.content:
The [b]All-mother[/b], the [i]Snake Woman[/i], and the demon of terrible omens, are some of the names associated with the famous goddess [b]Cihuacoatl[/b], or [i]Tonantzin[/i]. 

Ancient myths describe her as an [b]elusive [/b]woman, with her face painted red, wearing an eagle feather headdress and gold earrings.
A dual symbol of the origin of life, [b]maternity [/b]and care, but also of [b]war[/b], sacrifice and death. A beautiful embodiment of the neverending cycle between[b] life and death[/b].

It's believed that she used the bones [b]Quetzalcoatl [/b]brought back from the underworld in order to create life; she was the first being to ever [b]give birth[/b] and has warned her children of the coming of the Spaniards during Moteccuzoma's reign.

Her nightly [b]weeping [/b]along the streets warned the citizens of tragedies and [b]catastrophes [/b]to come. After all, there is nothing a mother wouldn't do for her children. 

What else is there to say about the WIP of this deity? Coming from the artist [b]Sergio [/b](aka "Perro Negro").

notes.title: Tlaxcaltecs
notes.content:
Out of all the people that the [b]Aztecs [/b]faced, none was so feared and respected as the [b]Tlaxcaltecs[/b], who were never subdued by them, and who allied themselves with the Spanish during the conquest of Mexico…
In today’s WIP, we show you the [b]clothings [/b]of a Tlaxcaltec warrior: the term [i]tlahuiztli [/i]originally referred to the clothing made of [b]feathers [/b]sewn over fabric, which covered the torso, arms and legs, but started to be used to refer to the [b]insignia [/b]that the warrior wore, as well as his arms and headdress.
When you fight the invaders on [i]Mictlan[/i], be prepared to come face to face with these strong and brave [b]warriors[/b], who will not ask or give any quarter.

notes.title: Blood bath
notes.content:
[b]Blood [/b]didn’t just serve as food for the gods, it also [b]strengthened [/b]and regenerated them…

Today we bring you this WIP in ultra-realistic 3D of the [b]priests [/b]that bathed [b]Mictlantecuhtli [/b]in blood.
 In pre-Columbian codices, it is narrated that a [b]ritual [/b]offered to such god of the underworld consisted of parts of a [b]body [/b]to be opened, such as: ears, tongues, thighs, wrists and/or calves, to fill containers with blood.
They were carried to the priests so they could [b]bathe the image[/b] of Mictlantecuhtli with this red liquid to be able to ask, for the whole town, [b]health [/b]for the ill or [b]rest [/b]for the dead.

notes.title: Tthe ruler of the Kupul
notes.content:
In this new WIP we can see the ruler of the [b]Kupul[/b], with their chief deity, [b]Kukulkan[/b]. 

The Kupul ruled one of the most important chiefdoms of the [b]Yucatan [/b]peninsula during the arrival of the Spanish, whose power sparked the fall of the city of Mayapan, which came before Chichen Itza. Kukulkan was the chief deity of the ruling lineage of the Kupul and served as the way (nahual) [b]guardian [/b]of their dynasty. 
The worshiping of Kukulkan was far common in the [b]theocratic [/b]society of the late Classic period and the [b]Postclassic [/b]period, where the cultural influences of the central region of Mexico fused with the beliefs of the [b]Maya[/b], sharing unique aesthetic and architectural styles that would be known as the international style of [b]Chichen Itza[/b].

notes.title: Itzpapalotl
notes.content:
Today we want to show you the concept art of [b]Itzpapalotl[/b], goddess of war, patroness of death, and councilor of the [b]Temoanchan Paradise[/b] (a mythical and earthly paradise).

The legend says that when Iztpapalotl was sent to Earth, falling from heaven, she wore an invisible cloak so that no one could see her, giving her the power of [b]invisibility[/b].

The fearsome [b]skeletal [/b]warrior goddess uses white makeup and different colors, and her chest pectoral represents [b]power and fire[/b].

Itzpapalotl appears with [b]butterfly [/b]or [b]eagle [/b]attributes. In our concept art, her hands and feet are replaced by jaguar claws, this makes her a Tzitzimitl “a mythical [b]terrible [/b]being”.

notes.title: Nahualli
notes.content:
This day is as mystical as the character of this WIP in 3D. We are talking about a [b]nahualli[/b], also known as a nagual; a human capable of transforming into an animal, who reveals the magical connection between [b]nature and spirituality[/b].

The ancestors spoke of how different peoples had a[b] guardian spirit[/b], as well as of how some humans were born with an animal self, which would use its powers and wisdom to trace their [b]destiny[/b]. 

Capable of great good and great evil, as well as communicating with both the dead and the gods, naguals were [b]emblematic characters[/b] of pre-Columbian culture, mystic beings with powers like healing and [b]divination[/b], that can still surprise us to this day.

Covered in the essence of the grackle, a black litmus feathered bird, with a screeching song and great intelligence, we introduce this powerful nagual to the [i]Mictlan [/i]family.

notes.title: Owl Man
notes.content:
In the original Nahua, [b]Tlacatecolotl [/b]means “Owl Man”; they are [b]dark sorcerers[/b], with the owl as their nagual, a harbinger of death and ill luck. 
They made a living from their malicious arts, usually cheating their victims, since they would [b]cast spells [/b]on them only to charge exorbitant prices to lift them. 
It’s not surprising then, that pre-Columbian authorities would [b]persecute [/b]Tlacatecolotl, or even avoid their infamous services whenever possible.
In this WIP we can see the[b] masked face[/b] of one of these fearsome necromancers, with his mask alluding to a great horned owl.

notes.content:
Today we want to show you the latest WIP of the entity known as [b]Tlacanexquimilli[/b]. Its name comes from the combination of the Nahuatl words [i]tlacaneci [/i](which means "without human form") and [i]quimilli [/i](meaning "bundle").
We can see some of the main features of this [b]otherworldly [/b]being, like its body having the shape of a mortuary bundle, using its many limbs to crawl on the ground. 
Seeing it was a [b]bad omen[/b], that would fill one's heart with fear and, eventually, succumb to either war or sickness; only the [b]bravest [/b]could endure looking at the Tlacanexquimilli.

notes.title: The temple of the Eagle and Jaguar warriors
notes.content:
Good day, travelers of [i]Mictlan[/i]! Today we have a WIP for you.

The[b] temple of the Eagle and Jaguar warriors[/b] was a place of initiation for the military elite of the Mexica Empire. It was directly carved on the stone of a mountain in the region of [b]Malinalco[/b], where the Mexica creation myths tell that the sister of Huitzilopochtli - Malinalxochitl - was abandoned by her brother in her pilgrimage to the Valley of Mexico. 

She founded the city that stood out for its talented [b]tlacuilos [/b]and its warm weather, that made it a place dedicated to art and the military and spiritual training for the Eagle and Jaguar warriors. 

In this WIP, we decided to show our “take” on this temple, adding sculptural elements from the time, with some [b]artistic freedom[/b] but with a strong basis on the [b]archeological remains[/b] so as not to lose its historical basis.

What do you think of this interpretation?

notes.title: Tlahuelpuchis
notes.content:
Our design team has brought you these WIP of the [b]Tlahuelpuchis[/b], whose design is based on Coyolxauhqui. 

The Tlahuelpuchis were common women that came into their powers after their first moonblood, although they could only achieve [b]transmutation into an animal [/b]through practice.

Tlahuelpuchis (also known as the “shining incense burner”) were considered naguals or [b]witches[/b], since sometimes they were seen as large fireballs. Today, they are associated with vampire women, since they feast on their victims’ blood, usually little children, who are marked by bruises and the bite of their fangs.

Good day, [i]Mictlantecs[/i]!

Today we bring you the 3D Model of the [b]Jaguar Warrior[/b], also known as [b]Ocepilli[/b], as one of the Jaguar Bosses. 

The design is a combination of fantasy elements and historical features, such as the jaguar pelt that honors this feline.
They were among the [u]highest-ranking fighters[/u] of the Mexica military structure. From the moment they turned seven years old they were taught the art of war, along with other lessons that explained the existence of the universe, of conscience and of life. 
They stood out for being rough, strong and, above all, [b]extremely brave[/b].

You may face them on your journey through [i]Mictlan[/i], as tank units capable of dishing out as much damage as they can endure.

notes.title: And then there was color
notes.content:
When [b]Aztlan [/b]was named “the white-colored country and dawn” every element of the life of our ancestors acquired a new tonality to describe its value. 

The relationship between colors and nature assigned the character of men, their actions and their language. Suddenly the temples carved from stone were dyed red, yellow, green or blue to honor the gods. 

The [b]Codices [/b]portrayed history with ink and the [b]warriors [/b]flew into battle with masks that illustrated their fierceness.

We’re excited to show you this WIP of the recovery of color for the vestiges of Mesoamerican culture. 
Currently, the temples and sculptures are shown without tones, so the [i]Mictlan [/i]team gathered the smallest details to honor what was essential for the lives of our ancestors, because life is always better with color.

notes.title: Tlamacazqui
notes.content:
In the Aztec religion, there were few people as important as the [b]priests[/b]. In Nahuatl, they were named [b]tlamacazqui[/b], which meant “giver of things”, and their role was to make sure that the gods received their due; be it offerings, ceremonies or sacrifices.

In today’s WIP, we’ll show you the concept art of a tlamacazqui based on the illustration of the [b]Codex Mendoza[/b].

The main accessories of a Mexica priest were the [b]xicolli [/b](an open vest that was opened from the front), as well as an incense burner, an incense bag, and a tobacco bar, which was used for religious purposes.

notes.title: Dual Teocallis
notes.content:
Good day, travelers of [i]Mictlan[/i]. 

The Mexica expansion through the Mesoamerican territory came hand in hand with the construction of [b]dual teocallis[/b], where the most important gods of the Mexica pantheon - Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc - were worshiped, as a way of [b]ideological imposition[/b] over the tributaries. 

As it was usual after every conquest, the gods of the subdued people were taken to Tenochtitlan as “captives” and then dual temples dedicated to the mentioned gods were built.

There are archeological remains of these temples of similar measurements to the[b] Templo Mayor[/b], such as the one of [b]Santa Ana Acatitlan[/b], which served us as a model for this WIP, to which we added some color tests.

Greetings, adventurers!

Today we show you the WIP of the [b]priest of Mictlantecuhtli[/b] on its 3D version.

This design is a fantasy take on popular pre-Columbian esthetic elements, as to give this character a more [b]terrifying [/b]appearance.

A very special feature is the[b] human skull [/b]the priest wears as decoration, which represents his relationship with the [b]god of death[/b].

There are several codices from the pre-Columbian and the colonial eras that mention these priests offering great deals of blood, copal, and even committing [b]self-sacrifice [/b](like cutting off their own ear lobes) in front of images of their chosen deity.

notes.title: Tecucizyo Tilmatli
notes.content:
We are pleased to show you this WIP of a character wearing the [b]Tecucizyo Tilmatli[/b], also known as the [b]snail cloak[/b], which was offered as tribute by the people of [b]Atlan[/b] and [b]Tuxpan[/b].

This cloak was a Mexica creation that carried a large artistic, symbolic and economic significance. It could be used in multiple ways and had several meanings; however, it was only worn by [b]men[/b].
The right to wear it was solely dependent on the [b]social status[/b] of each man, so they weren't just a simple garments; rather, they were seen as a symbol of [b]social power[/b].

It consisted of a large [b]rectangular cloth[/b] that was tied from two opposite sides, thus forming the [b]cape [/b]that would hang from either the back, the shoulder or the front of the wearer. These cloaks were woven in small towns all throughout the Huasteca region.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/cd0d2f3d349b544dc1b67af8263569520febbb0e.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/94c7c6970c6d300c23fec4d15ce0fec6cf52f75d.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/558626deff0a940ec5c3aea54199c6cb415f8013.png[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/8880a7b89f5bd3e7e67638dee77fdc74e6a22d0f.png[/img]

The Tecucizyo Tilmatli was mentioned in the [b]Codex Florentine[/b]. It bore the design of the cross-section of a sea snail, which symbolizes the [b]godly qualities of the moo[/b]n: regeneration, birth and fertility. 

Every 80 days, the residents of the Tuxpan province would offer 120 of these cloaks, woven from a burgundy dyed thread and with a double eye-shaped edging.

It’s said that the [b]Tlatoani [/b]himself would grant them as gifts to outstanding citizens and proficient fighters.

notes.title: The creation of a priest
notes.content:
Good day, [i]Mictlantecs[/i]!

Today, we present to you the WIP of the priest that will give you[b] glimpses of the future[/b] through your adventure on [i]Mictlan[/i].

His design is completely based on [b]fantasy[/b]. His clothing features a distinctive headdress and some bone accessories, which give him an imposing appearance.

During the [b]pre-Columbian era[/b], priests thought of themselves as an [b]extension of nature,[/b] so gaining worldly knowledge allowed each of them to better understand who they were, and vice versa.

History tells us that the Spanish were deeply [b]afraid[/b] of them, mostly because of their rituals, where they would perform [b]piercings and cuts [/b]on different parts of the body.

It is a[b] long process[/b] of development from the concept art to the final realization of a character: in this case, it started from our talented artist [b]marioricoart[/b], assisted by our chief historian, [b]Santiago[/b], continuing through our talented [b]3D team[/b] and our artist [b]Genaro[/b], and finally going through the hands of our creative director [b]Guillermo Alarcon [/b], sculpting his face.

notes.title: Chapel dedicated to the god Ehecatl
notes.content:
Here’s a new WIP modeled for you, travelers of [i]Mictlan[/i].

It was common for ancient [b]highly urbanized[/b] areas in Mesoamerica to be divided into several [b]Calpullis [/b](or districts) where entire families, dedicated to a [b]specific trade or craft[/b], lived. 
These districts had access to all available [b]services [/b]of the time, and had their own temples as well.

According to the economic capabilities of the inhabitants, these [b]temples [/b]could be as luxurious as the massive ceremonial centers of the nobles and the ruling class, or simple and modest, like the ones on the [b]macehualtin districts[/b]. In the case of this WIP, the temple is a chapel dedicated to the god [b]Ehecatl[/b], which features a round building, and a basement for mortuary niches. Small details like these make a difference in our work.

What do you think? Let us know in the comments!

Today, we have this WIP of a stone statue of the [b]god Xiuhtecuhtli[/b].
Considered as the “[b]Father of the Gods[/b]”, Xiuhtecuhtli was the god of fire, daytime and heat, as well as Lord of volcanoes in Aztec mythology.

notes.title: Temple of Xiuhtecuhtli
notes.content:
[i]Niltze[/i] (Hello), [b]Mictec family[/b]!

Today, the omens of an invasion manifest, and with it this #WIP of the [b]Temple of Xiuhtecuhtli [/b](the Old God, Lord of fire and heat).
Fatal auguries in the ancient codices tell of the coming of the Spanish, and in this occasion, we present to you the scene of the third sign: “[i]It didn’t rain hard, only drizzled slightly, and it wasn’t the heat from the sun, and there was no thunder either[/i]” This is what the inhabitants reported when they narrated how the sanctuary with a straw roof, called Xacal, burned up in flames.

What do you think, Mictecs? Do you know the other [b]fatal auguries[/b]?

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/18849f68ffe6cd62faf6604b007e68f6f8e64577.jpg[/img]

The [b]artistic expression[/b] of pre-Columbian culture didn’t have a limit: dance, music, painting and sculpture are some of the examples of the [b]ingenuity [/b]of our ancestors.
This WIP is part of the structure of the Temple of Xiuhtecuhtli, that sanctuary dedicated to the [b]God of Fire[/b]. The team of artists of Mictlan followed the ancient ways and recreated this sculpture that decorates the stairs of the sanctuary.

Did you like it? In [i]Mictlan [/i]we are interested in your opinions.

notes.content:

Today we present to you this WIP of the [b]Spanish nao[/b]s (also known as carracks) carrying the colors of the Hispanic monarchy. These designs, though based on history, were reimagined so they fit in the fantasy setting of [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i].
The naos were ships that the Spanish and Portuguese used to sail the waters of the Mediterranean and the North Atlantic seas, and were the main type of ship that the Spanish used in the [b]conquest of America[/b].
Being a [b]historical fantasy game[/b], the artistic team takes certain liberties in the designs of characters and items. 

Would you like to see more realistic designs? Or do you want something more fantasy, or something in between?

notes.title: Flyers of Papantla
notes.content:
Greetings, travelers of [i]Mictlan[/i]. It is with much pleasure that we present you this concept art, where you can see various reinterpretations of the [b]Flyers of Papantla[/b].

The Ritual of the Flyers, practiced in pre-Columbian times as a fertility ritual, was particularly important for the Aztecs. In this ritual the flyers danced in the air around a [b]human sacrifice[/b], a victim whose blood, when reaching the ground, assured a [b]bountiful harvest[/b].

While the fliers in bigger cities would have more ostentatious clothes, in this reinterpretation we can see them with simpler and more humble clothes, as they’re represented in the Codex Porfirio Díaz.

Which design do you like the most? [b]Tell us in the comments[/b]!

notes.title: Ixpuxtequi
notes.content:
Greetings, community!

Hoping you’re alright and safe. 

Today we show you the [b]3D study[/b] for the character [b]Ixpuxtequi[/b].

According to Nahua mythology, he was one of the four deities that inhabited the [b]underworld[/b]. His name meant “[b]broken face[/b]” and was represented as a human-shaped creature, but with eagle feet and without a lower jaw.
This is a being of [b]duality[/b], as it is considered a deity of fate, fortune and [b]luck[/b]; however, it’s also seen as a [b]dreadful monster [/b]and it’s feared due to the terrible things and bad luck it might inflict to lonely wanderers that cross its path late at night.

He was the husband of the goddess of fear and terror, [b]Nexoxcho[/b].

The time has come for all of you to meet this hellish creature,[b] Kiti Shraan[/b].

notes.title: Yohualtepoztli #3
notes.content:
The ones who dare to walk alone at night, might encounter one of the [b]most frightening beings[/b] in Tenochtitlan: a humanoid creature, that has no head. [b]Its chest is wide open[/b]: a revolting, bloody cavity displaying its heart, trapped in the ribcage.

You'll hear it coming, like an [b]axe [/b]being driven into wood.
That's where the name of the [b]Yohualtepoztli [/b]comes from: yohualli, “night”, and tepoztli, “axe”.

Faced with this creature, there's little you can to: either [b]flee [/b]or try to [b]rip its heart off[/b] its chest.

The destiny of whoever came upon it on the roads depended solely on the[b] strength of their character[/b].

You can see some of our [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2998826269362063607]concept art pieces here[/url]. And today, we have a little video to show you... [b]do you dare watch it[/b]?

notes.title: Tlacatecolotl
notes.content:
In the original Nahua, [b]Tlacatecolotl [/b]means “Owl Man”: they are dark sorcerers, with the owl as their [b]nagual [/b]([url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3110297119570303839]we talked about this here[/url]), a harbinger of death and ill luck. 

They made a living from their [b]malicious arts[/b], usually cheating their victims, since they would cast spells on them only to charge exorbitant prices to lift the curses. 
It’s not surprising then, that pre-Columbian authorities would [b]persecute [/b]Tlacatecolotl, or even avoid their infamous services whenever possible.

In this WIP we can see the masked face of one of these fearsome [b]necromancers[/b], with his mask reminding of a great horned owl.

notes.title: Heart extraction
notes.content:
Sacrificial rituals featuring human [b]heart extraction [/b]were a prevalent religious practice throughout ancient Mesoamerican societies, it was a way of establishing a [b]mystic connection[/b] between humans and the gods.
Stories from both the oral tradition and chronicles of the time remark the importance of this practice: the sacrificed victims were either [b]volunteers [/b]or [b]prisoners [/b]captured in the Flower Wars.

Here is a concept art piece from our talented team:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/7995e08b5a9a3839a071a1965932936071c4ea6c.jpg[/img]

Human sacrifices were usually performed at[b] sunrise [/b]or at [b]midday[/b], in accordance with the belief that blood replenished the solar cycle that gives life to the world.
However, there was a very special ceremony that was performed at [b]midnight[/b].

The ritual of [b]New Fire [/b]was celebrated every 52 years on the Huizachtepet, today called [i]Cerro de la Estrella[/i] (Hill of the Star), on Iztapalapa, in order to bless the coming Period; in this ritual, a human victim was offered, but only after all the [b]fires [/b]on all of Tenochtitlan and its surroundings were [b]put out[/b]. 

Once the sacrifice was completed, a fire was lit over the victim's head, which would then be shared throughout the city while everyone anxiously awaited the break of a new dawn, which would kickstart the next [b]52-years period[/b] and the endurance of the [b]Fifth Sun[/b].

notes.title: We keep expanding Mictlan
notes.content:
Reconstructing the ancient mythical tales of ancient México, it’s [b]not an easy task[/b].

Our [b]team of historians [/b]and archaeologists analyze the ancient monuments and historical evidence, then our [b]concept art team[/b] reconstructs Mesoamerican iconography and architecture mixing historical and fantasy elements to give life to ancient Mesoamerica in the 16th century! 

We’ve currently made[b] over 85 real-life-looking [/b] humans, monsters and mythical creature characters.
We've also created dozens of ancient [b]archaeological sites[/b] in Unreal Engine, sites from Tulum, Tenochtitlan, Tenochtitlan, Cholula and more, all within the expanded 45KM 2 square[b] open-world map [/b]of ancient Mexico (soon expanding to Central America!)

All of this in just less than 1 year in full development, including a 15-minute gameplay video ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3110297119570368253]have you seen it?[/url])!
Not bad for an indie studio with a low budget. Our strength is [b]our passion[/b] and [b]our community[/b]!

notes.title: The Chichimec
notes.content:
Today we’ll show you this WIP of a study of the [b]Chichimec facial paint[/b].
The Chichimec were a group of nomadic and semi-nomadic people that inhabited the territory known as Gran Chichimeca.
These feared Mesoamerican people were known for the human and animal [b]sacrifices [/b]that they practiced, as well as for their [b]skill [/b]and fierceness in war. 
They dressed with little clothing and body paint, and their warriors went to battle with face paintings (usually in white colors) to [b]intimidate their enemies[/b].

notes.title: DanyanCat as María de Estrada
notes.content:
Dear Mictlan community, we’re pleased to present you the WIP of [b]DanyanCat[/b] as [b]María de Estrada[/b], Spanish conquistador and member of Hernán Cortés’ expedition.

Shortly after being castaway in Cuba, she stayed in Mesoamerica looking for her husband, who was a member of Hernán Cortés’ hosts. De Estrada stood out as one of the few women that took an [b]active role [/b]in the conquest.
Chroniclers described her as a [b]brave [/b]and courageous woman, a fighter, skilled in using the sword, the roundel and spear, both on foot and horseback.

María de Estrada will be one of the historical characters that you will find in[i] Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i].

notes.title: Temple of Xochipilli
notes.content:
Hi, [i]Mictlantecs[/i]!

Today we want to show you the #WIP of the reconstruction of the [b]Temple of Xochipilli[/b].
Its design is based on a real structure found at the Templo Mayor in Mexico's City; the only part that was created by our artists is the oratory on top of the structure.

This place was dedicated to the god [b]Xochipilli[/b], which means “Prince of Flowers” or “Flowery Noble”. He was the god of flowers, love, games, beauty and pleasure. 

Have you checked [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3066366095787076821]our previous post[/url] about this god? You can see our [b]design [/b]and learn more about this important figure.

His temple was used for [b]celebrations [/b]in which the people of Tenochtitlan would bring lots of edible offerings, while Tenochtitlan’s neighbors would instead bring prisoners to be [b]sacrificed [/b]as tributes.

It is a pleasure and an honor for us to count on the support of a genius in the gaming world. [b]Jorge Levya[/b], pride of Tabasco, shares on this project his passion for video games, representing an important and respected figure in Mexica culture: [b]a great Tlatoani[/b].

There is no doubt that in Mexico there is great potential: the streamers, content creators, production team and players are the strength of this empire. 

Let the world know of the [b]Mexican potential[/b] in the gaming culture!

notes.title: Just a catch up
notes.content:
At [i]Mictlan[/i], every day we challenge ourselves as we try to improve our work pipeline.

When we started the project, our knowledge was very basic, but little by little we have improved the way we work as a team. [i]Mictlan [/i]is our first video game, most of our team does not have professional industry experience, making our efforts even more difficult. 
But the need to improve and learn our way of working has helped us to grow a lot, experimenting over and over again until we find favorable results. On one hand, this process delays our project, but on the other hand, ensures that we have the exact results that we are aiming for. 

[h3]We might be a small studio, but we have big aspirations![/h3]
 
The response of our community, your comments, your constructive feedback has also helped us a lot to improve our way of working and give ourselves new perspectives. We want to thank you for being here from the very beginning, for all the good vibes and constant support you've been providing us.

notes.title: Pyramid inspired to the House of Eagles
notes.content:
Hello, dear followers of [i]Mictlan[/i]!

Today we bring you this new WIP. Our artists created this [b]pyramid [/b]inspired by the[b] House of Eagles [/b]belonging to the archeological zone of Malinalco. 
This place's main purpose was to be a [b]sanctuary [/b]for the Eagle and Jaguar warriors to stay in, to rest between battles, to train their [b]fighting skills[/b], and to perform [b]sacred rituals[/b] related to witchcraft.

Inside the pyramids, there were three sculptures of birds and one of a feline, in addition to several stone bowls, which are believed to be used to[b] place the hearts[/b] of people that were sacrificed in the temple.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/892d759a38d18dc563cd3a8b8a43fba03b71cee6.jpg[/img]

notes.title: Black Temple
notes.content:
Today we are presenting concept art pieces of the[b] Black Temple[/b], right out of the imagination of our talented artist [b]Mauricio Pampin[/b].

In this temple, [b]Micltantecutli[/b]’s priests would worship him by sacrificing prisoners.
We can see where the points of interest will be located in the temple, like the sacrificial table or Mictlantecuhtli’s effigy, as well as the scale of the walls and columns in relation to the player’s character.

In order to accomplish this kind of works, our artists need to carry extensive research on [b]pre-Columbian architecture[/b], and then mix reality and historical accuracy with the[b] dark fantasy elements[/b] that will give this place a surreal, frightening look.

notes.title: Cihuacoatl
notes.content:
Today we want to show you the first concept arts for the Mexica deity [b]Cihuacoatl[/b].

The “snake woman” is a deity associated with earth and its fertility under the name of Quilaztli; but perhaps her biggest qualities are her [b]prophetic abilities [/b]and her intimate relationship with power as a complementary figure to Huitzilopochtli.

The temple of Cihuacoatl was known as the [b]House of Blackness[/b], and in some texts, there were stories about how it was necessary to crawl into a space of complete darkness where she resided.

notes.title: Flyers of Papantla
notes.content:
Today we are presenting you the[b] Flyers of Papantla[/b], those who performed the ancient [b]Ritual of the Flyers[/b].

The origin of this ritual is a [b]prayer to a deity[/b] as a way to ask for the rain to fall over the crops in times of drought. It was a [b]fertility dance[/b] full of symbolism, originally associated with the region of Totonacapan in Veracruz.

These participants to the Ritual of the Flyers, in Pre-Columbian times, are wearing more [b]simple clothes[/b], they are possibly from a more rural area, isolated from the [b]urban centers[/b] where these rituals would have the proper flair of an event of this magnitude.

notes.title: Tepechichi
notes.content:
Hello, travelers of [i]Mictlan[/i]!

Today we present to you the concept art a [b]nocturnal and reclusive [/b]creature which, when sighted by the Spanish, was reported and drawn in the colonial manuscripts as a [b]ferocious beast[/b]... but it was just a [b]ferret[/b]!

This is the [b]Tepechichi[/b], translated from Nahuatl as "dog of the wilds" or "old man of the wilds". It’s an animal with piercing black eyes, prominent and pointy teeth, a thin and long body of thick grayish fur. 

Thanks to its sharp and retractile claws, it is capable of [b]climbing trees and walls[/b] with great ease.

Be [b]careful [/b]and pay attention on your journey, because this agile and [b]naughty [/b]being can appear at any time…

notes.content:
The[b] Black Temple [/b]is the place where the worshippers of Mictlantecuhtli reunite to perform the [b]secret rituals[/b].

notes.title: Obsidian weapons
notes.content:
The [b]weapons [/b]used by our indigenous Mesoamerican [b]ancestors [/b]were usually made from [b]wood and stone[/b], which made it even more difficult for the indigenous people to defend themselves against the [b]Spanish soldiers[/b].

One of the most important and iconic materials used in Mesoamerican cultures was [b]obsidian[/b], a volcanic stone somewhat similar to glass that could easily tear through flesh. Many tools were made with this material, from [b]ceremonial daggers[/b] to mighty weapons, such as the [b]macuahuitl[/b].

notes.title: Two great temples
notes.content:
Today we want to show you some sketches from the megalithic [b]temple of Malinalco[/b], how it could have looked in its prime.
Malinalco was an [b]ideological and spiritual center[/b] for the Mexica Empire; it was the place where the sister of Huitzilopochtli, Malinalochitl, had settled when abandoned by his brother during a long pilgrimage of the Aztec people to the Valley of Mexico. And in this specific place, they prepared and commanded the eagle and jaguar warriors, the [b]elite militia[/b] from the Mexica army.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/283acf3e5c8b1d1918cada71f14e9124f59851d1.jpg[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/2cd5c828462d39771e2f90a1a24b3ef0d92f63d7.jpg[/img]

We also want to share with you the excellent work from our friend and collaborator [b]Mauricio Pampin[/b], who, on the basis of the postclassic aesthetic, built from zero a [b]great temple dedicated to Mictlantecuhtli[/b].
We know that the sanctuaries of Tenochtitlan played an important role, not only in the sacred area. In the “Calpulli” slums, sacred houses were built for the gods, where they held rituals to maintain the balance of the world.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/e6a0a5453a56004676660ac7db76b4a01207f415.jpg[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/be86cf7d282fe3d7e653cdc61f47431a83f27e9d.png[/img]

notes.title: The Mictecas
notes.content:
Every God has its [b]servants[/b]. 

[b]Xochiquetzal [/b]had an entourage of minions that liven up his celestial court; 

[b]Tlaloc [/b]had his loyal Tlaloques who could send down to the earth different kinds of rain, and Mictlantecuhtli… had the [b]Mictecas[/b].

The Mictecas were the first inhabitants of Mictlan, the most loyal [b]lieutenants [/b]of the lord of the dead. They were the [b]agents of the underworld[/b], in charge of preventing anyone from leaving the world of Mictlan. Mictecas [b]devoured [/b]the dead on their way to the nine regions of Mictlan, they were also the ones who would [b]go to battle[/b] when their god commanded them.

Are you willing to fight the[b] terrible legions [/b]of Mictlantecuhtli?

notes.title: Mayan priesthood
notes.content:
The early Maya [b]priesthood [/b]consisted of a [b]hierarchy [/b]of professional priests serving as intermediaries between the population and the deities. They were men of great culture and wisdom.

The ones at the top of the hierarchy were called [b]Sun priests[/b], they presided over rituals wearing beautiful tunics, covered in animal fur and gold. 

On the second level were the [b]Chilan[/b], prophets that went into trance to predict the future.

Another important figure in the Mayan culture were the [b]ah-men,[/b] or doctors/physicians.
Ah-men were responsible for keeping a [b]balance [/b]in life with nature and the spirits. During Mayan ceremonies, they used the aromatic resin called [b]copal[/b], sacred liquor, porcupine quills and herbs to invoke the four Cardinal points, summoning the [b]heart of the sky[/b], with powerful prayers spoken in the Mayan language.

notes.content:
In this new image, you can see the ruler of the Kupul, with his chief deity, [b]Kukulkan[/b]. 

The Kupul ruled one of the most important chiefdoms of the [b]Yucatan peninsula[/b] during the Spanish conquest, whose power caused the fall of the city of Mayapan, which came before Chichen Itza.

Kukulkan was the chief deity of the ruling lineage of the Kupul. His name translates as the [b]Feathered Serpant[/b]. The worshiping of Kukulkan was far common in the theocratic society of the [b]late Classic period[/b] and the Postclassic period, where the cultural influences of the central region of Mexico fused with the beliefs of the [b]Maya[/b], sharing unique aesthetic and architectural styles that would be known as the international style of [b]Chichen Itza[/b].

This is just a [b]work in progress[/b], but we're glad to share with you what we're constantly creating to give life to the world of [i]Mictlan[/i]!

notes.content:
[b]Music[/b], dances and special rituals will be featured in [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i].

Among other game assets, our wonderful 3D modeling team has been working on several [b]musical instruments[/b], including the [b]Tlapitzalli tubular flute[/b].

notes.content:
Today we want to show you a very important and revealing [b]concept art[/b]...

The [b]entrance[/b] to the dreaded underworld, the realm of [i]Mictlan[/i]!

This is the realm of [b]Mictlantecutli [/b]and, according to the scarce historical references, it is believed that it has [b]four entrances[/b]: one for each cardinal point, with the main one being on the west, where each day dies...

notes.title: Nao (ships)
notes.content:
Did you know that the [b]nao [/b]were an evolution of the coca ships that, at the same time, descended from the Viking [b]knarr merchant ships[/b]?

The nao were born from the necessity of making[b] new discoveries [/b]during the trips made by the European explorers on their routes to Asia, Africa and America. 

The [b]caravels[/b], ships used by Christopher Columbus on his voyage to the West Indies, despite being suitable for long-distance maritime voyages, began to [b]fall into disuse[/b] due to the demands for bigger cargos and better ways of transportation for the resources, demands which became increasingly more pressing. This situation led to the creation of [b]new and improved boats[/b], making the bow and stern castles wider and higher, as well as providing them with a greater load capacity.

In this WIP you can see three models of the Spanish nao´s, based on [b]paintings [/b]of the time as well as [b]contemporary reconstructions[/b].

notes.title: Stone Gloves
notes.content:
We have been working on developing a character whose main weapons are [b]stone gloves[/b], but do you know what did the pre-Hispanic gloves look like?

To answer this question, we must go back to the amazing work of [b]Taube and Zender[/b], [i]American gladiators: ritualistic boxing in ancient Mesoamerica[/i], where we can find several representations of brawlers and gloves made out of [b]shells, bones or stone[/b].

The use of these gloves is shared among the Olmec, Zapotec and Maya cultures and it is also featured in the outfit of some [b]gods [/b]such as Chaac, who wears a great stone glove which he uses to[b] light up the sky [/b]during storms.

notes.title: High Hierarchy Shaman
notes.content:
Greetings, [i]Mictlantecas[/i]!

Today we want to show you this WIP of the [b]elder healer[/b] who is being developed by our concept artists. As you can see, she is a [b]high hierarchy shaman[/b]. 

She carries some herbs, bones, mushrooms, peyotes and other stuff, useful for her creations. Her [b]mantle [/b]is made of vegetable fibers (such as maguey and palm tree) and her [b]staff [/b]is made of Ahuehuete wood.

This healer also has[b] experience in battle[/b], so we think that her potions and recipes could help the player with their offensive skills, or maybe give them more strength and agility, or even make their spells more powerful...?

Whatever will be, make sure to find you a [b]good healer[/b]!

notes.title: Tlazolteotl
notes.content:
[b]Tlazolteotl[/b] (originally a deity of Huasteco origin) found a relevant place among the Mexica deities. She represented the different forms of [b]passion[/b], and that is why she was the goddess of [b]fertility [/b]and births.

Her help was sought as a goddess of carnal love, but it could cause unbridled[b] sexual appetites[/b]. She protected midwives and pregnant women, and her image was placed at the entrance of the temazcales where she was called “[b]Grandmother of temazcal[/b]”.

She was related to the goddess [b]Toci[/b], the mother of the gods, also known as "Heart of the earth" or "Entrails of the earth" because she [b]fostered life[/b] and cared for her children (gods, men, animals or plants).

Tlazolteotl was also know as "[b]Eater of filth"[/b] since she had the ability to [b]purify[/b] the bodies of sexual offenders if they performed acts of confession and sacrifice. As a matter of fact, Tlazoteotl is often depicted with her mouth and chin darkened from [b]consuming filth and sins[/b].

notes.title: Wisdom of Our Elders
notes.content:
Today we are showing you a [b]concept art[/b] for an older [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2868219761330979442]healer [/url]you will encounter in [i]Mictlan[/i].

The wise elders will have [b]more ingredients[/b] available and maybe [b]more potions[/b] and recipes to craft. In this design, we rely on a [b]fantasy [/b]look, equipping them with a staff that they use to invoke magical powers in some special rituals, asking for the gods' intervention. For example, a ritual for Tlaloc to summon a [b]hailstorm[/b], or a ritual for Huehueteotl to summon a [b]rain of fire.[/b]

This design is still a WIP, but you know what to expect in [i]Mictlan[/i]: you'll have to find these elder healers and [b]uncover their secrets[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/2212f8f54f406aef1c427b711e36d3294615908a.jpg[/img]

The [b]oral tradition[/b] is very important for the Mesoamerican cultures. The elders are the keepers of history, and their word is respected and honored.

In this other piece of concept art, you can see an elder [b]telling all sorts of stories[/b]. He bears battle scars as if he is carrying the [b]weight of war and history[/b] on his shoulders while hiding the [b]truth [/b]behind his penetrating eyes.

In [i]Mictlan [/i]you’ll have to seek these characters to get information about the myths and ancient traditions, maybe to find a [b]special temple [/b]or to [b]summon a deity[/b].

The Spaniards will be an enemy to fear in the open territories, and you will have to adapt your strategy to deal with the soldiers in the long distances.

notes.title: Priests of the pre-Hispanic world
notes.content:
The priests of the pre-Hispanic world had a pretty[b] hard life[/b]. 

[b]Penance, pain and sacrifice[/b] were part of their daily routine. 

They were the ones who ripped off the hearts of the victims in services. 
They were the ones who read the oracles to the Kings on the most important matters. 
They anointed the Kings once they were elected. 

The sacrifices made by the priests would feed the gods and ensure the continued existence of the world.

The [b]high priest [/b]was always the second son of the King. These figures had a great reputation for their [b]holiness [/b]and observed a rather rigid and austere conduct, from childhood.

notes.title: Mictlan's weapons
notes.content:
Today we want to show you a set of designs of the[b] indigenous weapons [/b]that have been recreated by our concept artists.

Did you know about the lethality of the indigenous weapons in the pre-Hispanic world? 
[b]Let us tell you about it[/b]!

The many weapons that the indigenous people wielded needed to be mastered in order to be used to their [b]full potential[/b]; which is why the younger people were trained in their use from a relatively[b] early age[/b].

The [b]atlatl[/b], the[b] stone axes[/b], the [b]macuahuitl [/b]and the [b]obsidian knives[/b], are some of the weapons recorded by the chroniclers and researchers, who highlighted the remarkable characteristics of obsidian, deadly because of its sharpness and its splinters.

In [i]Mictlan [/i]you will be able to find these weapons and master them, to open your way through the deep underworld while you face [b]Spaniards[/b], rival [b]indigenous people[/b] and [b]supernatural creatures [/b]of Mesoamerican mythology.

notes.title: Incense for the deities
notes.content:
Did you know that the Mexica priests had to light up [b]incense [/b]for the effigies of their gods[b] four times a day[/b]?

Among the many tasks they had, the Mexica novices and priests were in charge of burning a [b]special resin[/b] called [b]copal[/b], which was extracted from one of two kinds of [b]busera trees[/b]. This resin was burned in small [b]incense burners[/b], which came in many different shapes, the most common ones having an elongated shape that ended with a [b]circle [/b]at the center for depositing the copal.

The chronicles tell about the general uses for copal, in public, domestic and private ceremonies for [b]commoners as well as nobles[/b].

The [b]tlamacazque [/b]offered the copal smoke directing it towards the [b]four cardinal points[/b], towards the [b]Sun [/b]and finally towards the image of a [b]deity[/b], with the purpose of linking men and gods, so the latter would favor the former. 

[b]This practice survived [/b]the Spanish conquest, as the use of copal is still present in many indigenous festivities of modern-day Mexico.

This image shows a tlamacazque, with his body painted black, carrying a bag containing copal, and an incense burner, which is based on those found in a massive offering of burners at the[b] Greater Temple[/b] in Mexico’s City.

[h3]Have you ever enjoyed the fragrant smell of copal?[/h3]

notes.title: Mexican priesthood
notes.content:
Do you know the different ranks of the [b]Mexican priesthood[/b]?

The[b] Florentine Codex[/b] is a document created especially for the King Carlos V and was overseen by [b]Fray Bernardino de Sahagún[/b], written thanks to the tales of survivors of the conquest. The document represents in a pictographic nature the culture, society, customs and history of the [b]Mexica people[/b], a valuable document in the studies of ancient Mexico.

In this document, the [b]different ranks[/b] that existed among the Mexica priests are described:

“The ranks, by which one would rise, were as follows: the first was called tlacamazto, an acolyte; the second was called tlamacazquj, a deacon; the third, they called him tlenamacac, a priest. From these priests, the best ones were considered as supreme pontiffs and they were called ‘quequetzalcoa’, which means heirs of Quetzalcoatl”.

Based on this information, we have another WIP variant of what a Tlamacazqui or a deacon could be, based on the Durán Codex, where the priests are offering [b]human hearts [/b]to a giant image of the god [b]Mictlantecuhtli[/b].

notes.title: Deadlier than weapons...
notes.content:
Contrary to traditional beliefs, the best weapon available for the Spanish against the indigenous people were neither firearms, breastplates nor horses. 

The[b] plagues[/b] and diverse [b]diseases [/b]were the main causes for the demographic decline.

Diseases like [b]smallpox [/b]spread quickly through the American population, with no distinction between kings and peasants. Death traveled the land and nothing could stop the ruthless and devastating virus that spared no one.

In this concept art, we display the picture of workers infected by smallpox, an image that became common at the beginning of the conquest, until the surviving indigenous people were able to generate the necessary [b]antibodies [/b]and survive the disease.

notes.title: Coyote Warriors
notes.content:
Did you know that [b]Coyote warriors[/b] existed both with the Mexica and the Tlaxcalans?

The Coyote warrior appears numerous times in the History of Tlaxcala, participating on the side of the Mexica, as well as the Tlaxcalan. It also appears in Mixtec codices and in Teotihuacan murals. 

It was a creature of a [b]carnivorous nature and great libido[/b], and was associated with the immutable cycle of regeneration and death, the base of the Mesoamerican cosmovision; so it is not surprising that it sought to have its own power and strength, just as it was for the eagle and jaguar warriors.

The coyote was so important that the name of [b]Nezahualcoyotl[/b], an extraordinary character in Mesoamerican history (a poet, reformer, warrior and lover) means “[b]fasting coyote[/b]”.

This is why for this WIP we present a coyote warrior, in this case, a [b]fire coyote[/b], represented in the first memoirs. We based its shield on one of the few Mesoamerican shields that have survived to this day, besides adding multicolored plumage, representing the [b]noble background [/b]of the character.

notes.title: Priests of Mictlantecuhtli
notes.content:
Did you know that the priests of [b]Mictlantecuhtli [/b]had their hair tangled up to look like the beings from the [b]underworld[/b]?

In an archeological context, there has been found only [b]one temple [/b]that worshipped Mictlantecuhtli, and that is the “Templo de las Calaveras”. It was found in 2013 while excavating the archaeological zone of Tehuacán El Viejo, in the state of Puebla. This temple stands out because it has ornaments made of [b]human skulls [/b]embedded on its sidewalls, as well as images of this deity where the shrine once stood, making it one of a kind.

In the iconographic reference, we have several pre-Hispanic and colonial codices where they present the priests of Mictlantecuhtli offering large quantities of [b]blood [/b]or performing the [b]self-sacrifice[/b]. 

Alternatively, in the tonalamatl books such as the codex Cospi, a priest of Mictlantecuhtli is shown offering copal and blood from his ears to a temple dedicated to the deities of the night.

Based on these somewhat limited references, we took some “liberties” to represent this WIP of a priest of Mictlantecuhtli. He stands out for his “dirty” look, possibly due to the [b]arduous religious rites[/b] associated with human sacrifice, with his tangled up hair in honor of his tutelary deity, and with a feather ornament that holds his long dreadlocks, as well as a clay container, where [b]human hearts[/b] were collected.

As a final touch, in a more fantastic twist, he carries a [b]scepter [/b]with a human skull, emphasizing his relationship with the fearsome [b]god of death[/b].

notes.title: Spanish soldiers' equipment
notes.content:
[i]Mictlan [/i]is set in Mesoamerica, during the 16th century, in the early days of the [b]expedition of Cortes[/b]. Therefore, our academic team and our very talented conceptual artists have tried to [b]reconstruct [/b]with chronicles, studies and archaeological traces the history of the time, including the[b] first members [/b]of Hernan Cortes' company.

The soldiers of the 16th century were equipped with the [b]latest tools and weapons[/b], with the introduction of [b]firearms[/b], therefore battle strategies were gradually changing. Still, [b]other weapons [/b]also proved to be very useful, the best example being the sword, spear, halberd and crossbow.

According to [b]Lopez de Gomara's chronicle[/b], the Spaniards were mostly armed with swords and daggers, in accordance with the data collected by Sahagún and Bernal Díaz del Castillo's own account. 

As for their [b]clothing[/b], it varied according to their socioeconomic condition, as some were able to afford iron breastplates, while others would be left with simpler protections.

notes.title: The Wise Elder
notes.content:
[b]Old age [/b]was a very important stage for pre-Hispanic cultures, it was believed that the elderly were those who knew the [b]truth[/b] and could transmit it to those around them.

The old men were considered wise, with incredible mental strength. Many times, they fulfilled the role of [b]advisers and guides[/b] in celebrations and rituals, always knowing the appropriate moment to act or not to act.

With all references we studied, our artists were inspired to create this concept art of an [b]Elder Sage[/b], a character with a certain mastery over nature and time.

He carries a plume of feathers and natural fibers, he also wears a cloth and fur cloak matching with his [i]maxtlatl[/i], both with wooden and leather finishes. His staff ends with a deer antler.

The Elder Sage can teach the players [b]important lessons[/b] inside the universe of [i]Mictlan[/i], help you to [b]summon gods[/b], reveal secrets about nahual transformation and about your journey to the underworld.

notes.content:
Spaniards and indigenous people had various [b]confrontations [/b]throughout the conquest period, in the different regions of Latin America.

In the case of Mesoamerica, diplomatic relations were always the first battlefields, since the support from indigenous subjects of the triple alliance was essential for the fall of the Mexica culture.

In this concept art shows a fight presenting various elements that set the tone of the [b]clashes between Spaniards and indigenous people[/b], including new tools such as horses and metal protections.
[b]
Terrible battles[/b] unfolded under the wing of the conquest and you as a player will be able to relive some of them in the adventure that awaits you in [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i].

notes.title: Serpent Warlock
notes.content:
Today we want to share a story, maybe a legend...

Before the conquest of Mexico, a boy was born in San Andrés Chinantla, the modern-day state of Puebla. He would be called [b]Xiuhcoatl[/b], which means [b]jade serpent[/b], after one of the most beautiful stones in North America, but which is also the name for the [b]mythical weapon [/b]on the god Huitzilopochtli.

From a very young age, the boy displayed [b]magical abilities[/b]: it is said that he was born from the earth while illuminated by the stars and that he was [b]immortal[/b]. It is also said that, while still in diapers, he would fade and reappear as a [b]snake[/b], playing tricks and pranking everyone he met.

His father was a successful merchant, while his mother was a known priestess. 

Xiuhcoatl would live to [b]protect his people[/b].

notes.title: The Arquebus
notes.content:
The [b]matchlock arquebus [/b]is a classic weapon of the conquest, with ample documented evidence that indicates its early arrival to the American continent.

According to Bernal Díaz del Castillo, [b]Hernán Cortés[/b] used these weapons to incentivize other Spaniards to join his expedition, which suggests that a cache of these weapons was readied for the expedition towards the lands of the Yucatan. The same expedition would go into the Mesoamerican territory and face the Mexica Empire.

Contrary to common belief, most times the arquebus was (not literally) a double edge sword; though its [b]reach and power[/b] surpassed by far the bows and atlatl, its reload time was slower, allowing at least 20 arrows to be shooted and there was always the possibility that the powder would be ruined by the humid weather.

Here we present a design for a weapon you will find in [i]Mictlan[/i]. You will be able to choose between a more [b]nimble and silent [/b]weapon such as a bow or an atlatl, or one that is[b] far more lethal[/b], although slower, such as an arquebus.

notes.title: Mexica priests #2
notes.content:
Did you know that the [b]Mexica priests[/b] dyed their temples red using the[b] blood of the sacrifices[/b] made for the gods?

The priestly [b]garments [/b]worn during the celebrations of the festivities dedicated to gods were[b] varied and complex[/b], but during the days when their tutelary deities were not honored by all the common people, the priests dressed in a more [b]humble way[/b], with a [i]xicolli [/i]or nightgown, painting their body with black and smearing their hair with blood, then proceeded to clean themselves every night, except if they were performing some [b]penance[/b], in which fasting and sacrifices ordered them to maintain that aspect for days or weeks.

Check out [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2951535720199796614]our previous posts[/url] about Mexica priests!

In [i]Mictlan [/i]we constantly seek to create a [b]faithful vision[/b] of the pre-Hispanic world, as well as maintaining a balance with the [b]fantastic elements [/b]that make every video game a masterpiece.

What do you think, folks?

notes.title: Aztec buildings repurposed by another faith
notes.content:
Did you know that when the Spanish conquistadors conquered Tenochtitlan in 1521, they immediately destroyed one of the [b]most important temples[/b] in the city to make room for what would become the principal [b]Christian church[/b] in the capital of New Spain? 

This became a common practice, and over 68 churches [b]were built over[/b] prehispanic buildings that had sacred meaning to the indigenous people.

notes.title: The seventh omen: a mythical bird
notes.content:
Did you know that the seventh and penultimate [b]omen [/b]of the fall of Tenochtitan was a[b] bird with a mirror on its head[/b]?

This omen was witnessed by Moctezuma II himself, and the chronicles tell of his encounter with this strange being, a harbinger of the gods to[b] warn him of the final fall[/b].

“Something was caught in the nets. The hunters caught a certain[b] ashen bird [/b]like a crane. Then they went to show it to Motecuhzoma, at the House of Black (the house of magical studies). The Sun had reached its highest point: it was midday. There was something similar to a [b]mirror on the bird's head[/b]: it was as if it had a perforation on its middle point.
That night, people could see the sky, the stars, the Mastelejo (comet). Motecuhzoma interpreted this as a [b]bad omen[/b]. Then, when he looked at the bird’s head a second time, he saw in the background something that looked like a group of [b]people [/b]who were running, in a rush, shoving each other. They fought among themselves and were carried by some kind of deers. In that instant, Motecuhzoma called his wizards, his sages. He said to them: "What have I seen?" The sages were searching for an answer, tried to see something. But [b]everything was gone[/b], they saw nothing.”

For this WIP we present to you this mythical bird, but in place of a simple obsidian mirror on the top of its head, we chose to place a[b] broken obsidian crystal[/b], where those ominous visions would be reflected, heightening the[b] supernatural features[/b] of this bird.

notes.title: The Jaguar Warlock
notes.content:
The jaguar was one of the most [b]worshipped beings[/b], not only by the Mexica but also by almost all of the Mesoamerica people. It was said that those who were born on the day of "océlotl" would be the best at war, that they would show their courage and strength.

It is also claimed that there were people who were capable of transforming into the [b]powerful felines[/b], who could acquire superhuman strength and knowledge.

With this inspiration and stories in mind, our artists have created this fantastic concept of the [b]Jaguar Warlock[/b], a character who expresses all of his power through the fur clothing with the characteristic spotted design of the jaguar, but who also has a mystical aura, like the jaguar himself, [b]lord of all animals[/b].

We have not yet defined his powers or abilities, but perhaps you, community of [i]Mictlán [/i]can help us. What else would you like to see about this character? 

He will surely be a very powerful ally or... [b]enemy[/b].

notes.content:
The mythical world of [i]Mictlan [/i]is wide and it includes deities that could [b]terrify anyone [/b]just with their aspect… 

Such is the case of the [b]Tzizimine[/b] (take a look at [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3029213935088677469]our previous concept art[/url]).

Women-like creatures, with rotten, [b]decaying flesh [/b]which reveal the skeleton underneath, with clawed hands and feet, wearing ornaments made of skull necklaces and human hearts.

The Tzizimine are [b]nocturnal deities[/b] whose purpose was to devour human beings at the end of the Fifth Sun. They would descend from the sky at night and stalk the little kids to kidnap them. They would also appear during the eclipses to eat the sun and swallow the entire humanity.

notes.title: The final attack on Tenochtitlan
notes.content:
The [b]final attack on Tenochtitlan [/b]was carried by the joint actions on the roadways with the support of brigs, for which the Mexica canoes were no match. Little by little, the Spanish army, empowered by a growing number of allies, enclosed the [b]brave Mexica[/b], who were still capable of causing a lot of damage before their surrender, caused by a combination of superior weaponry by the Spanish and devastating diseases which had been spread.

August 13th of 1521, after a siege that lasted over 2 months, [b]the city was besieged [/b]and the last emperor, Cuahutemoc, was captured as he tried to make his escape aboard a canoe.

Cortés’s victory[b] destroyed the Aztec empire[/b], and the Spanish began to consolidate control over what became the colony of New Spain.

Take a look at the conceptual image designed by our talented Mexican artist [b]Mauricio Pampin [/b]of this historic moment.

notes.title: Mayan women: a study
notes.content:
Did you know that [b]Mayan women[/b] liked perfume and a daily bath with cold water?

In [i]Yucatan at the Time of the Spanish Encounter[/i] by Fray Diego de Landa, chapter XXXI mentions the following about the cosmetics and clothing of Mayan women:

[quote]Their noses were pierced through the small square that divides the windows in the middle to put an amber stone in the hole and had it as an ornament.
They pierced their ears to put on earrings in the same way of their husbands; carved their body from the waist up, except for the breasts.

The Indian women of the provinces of Bacalar and Campeche dressed very modestly. The breasts were covered by tying the clothes under the armpits using a folded blanket. All the others did not wear any clothing other than a long and wide jacket open on both sides.[/quote]

O the basis of the descriptions and reconstructions from the murals, codex vessels and clay figures by Daniel Parada (Aka Zotz), we shaped our own study of what a[b] noble and commoner woman of Yucatan[/b] would look like during the period of the Spanish conquest. Moving away from the stereotypes present in Apocalypto, seeking a respectful balance between[b] historical authenticity and fantasy[/b].

What do you think?

notes.title: The third omen
notes.content:
For the Aztecs, [b]omens [/b]were important events that predicted [b]danger of the empire[/b].  

For ten years before the arrival of Cortés and his men, the Aztecs witnessed various omens that supposedly [b]foretold the end of the empire[/b].

​The third omen was when a[b] bolt of lightning[/b] hit the temple of the god of fire, Xiuhtecuhtli. Sahagun sources indicate that the bolt of lighting had [b]no thunder nor sound[/b] associated with it. The inexorable fire and flames overcame the temple and [b]destroyed it[/b].

In this WIP you can see the exact moment when that event took place. To add [b]more drama[/b] to the scene,  we opted for a [b]night scenario[/b], deviating a bit from the chronicles.

notes.title: Ahuizotl #2
notes.content:
Dear [i]Mictlan [/i]fans, today we want to show you a preview of one of [i]Mictlan[/i]'s legendary creatures, the [b]Ahuizotl[/b]. 

"[b]Espinoso de agua[/b]'' (Thorny One of the Water) is the meaning of its name in Nahuatl. It was the size of a coyote, with small pointed ears, a long tail and a kind of human hand at the end of the tail. 

This creature lived in the deep springs of the waters, [b]hunting many fishermen's sleep[/b].

It would use its long, prehensile tail to grab its [b]unsuspecting victims[/b] to pull them under the water. It would hold them there, until they drowned. The Ahuizotl would then[b] feast on[/b] its prey's eyes, nails and teeth, leaving the rest of the body floating in the water.

notes.title: Mexica warrior
notes.content:
The Mexica culture was famous for its monumental architecture, complex society, and sacrificial rites. 

Nonetheless, pre-HIspanic cultures were also recognized for their militaristic power, standing out in the chronicles of the 16th century as [b]fearsome warriors[/b], who gave a hard time to the Spaniards during the first years of the conquest.

Amongst the most iconic images of their culture are the [b]warriors of Tenochtitlan[/b]: the Jaguar and Eagle warriors, elite troops that in their early days, were young macehualli who captured enemies, perfecting themselves battle after battle, until achieving [b]mastery[/b].

This is a concept art of a [b]Mexica warrior[/b] ready for battle in [i]Mictlan[/i]!

Every landscape, character and artifact that you find will be registered as your own [b]codex[/b], which you will be able to access any time you want and learn a bit more about them.

In [i]Mictlan [/i]you will be able to visit the city in its [b]maximum splendor[/b]; a city that the Mayans designed as a quadrilateral, so that the four corners are oriented with the cardinal points (you can take a look [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2969546585727991779]at these pictures[/url] that we already posted!).

notes.title: Macuiltochtli
notes.content:
[b]Macuiltochtli[/b], the god symbol of [b]excess and over-indulgence[/b], presented to you in a new variation. 

The [b]Sahagún [/b]informants describe him with a fine featherwork headdress, facial paint in the shape of a hand, crystal ornaments and an obsidian hatchet. He also carries an enormous calabash filled to the brim with the first [i]pulque[/i], the one that was made by Mayahuel and Patecatl. 

As he pours one jicara shell after another for himself, he claims that there is [b]no finer drink [/b]than true [i]pulque[/i], the one hailing from Chichinautzin.

Thanks to the unparalleled creativity of our art team, all the historical references have been fused with [b]fantasy elements[/b], as is distinctive of our style, in order to create this kind of character.

What do you think? Do you like it?

notes.title: Itzmitlanapochcalocan
notes.content:
Beyond [b]Chiconiahuapan [/b](the place of the nine rivers) there's a place known as [b]Itzmitlanapochcalocan[/b], the final step of the journey for all of those who have entered the jaws of the earth. 

This great chamber, at the deepest levels of [b]Mictlan[/b], is home to Mictlantecuhtli and Mictecacihuatl, the couple who [b]reigns the underworld[/b].

Historical sources describe it as an incredibly[b] dark place [/b]without an exit, where the last offerings are given to the supreme rulers.

The artistic genius of our [b]concept artists [/b]brings us a fantastic new vision applied to this mythical abyss. Here, the flames summoned by Mictlantecuhtli are the only light guiding us to his throne, a monument to the power of the god of death, made with the skeleton of a [b]gigantic being from a past era[/b].

notes.title: Pentamuti
notes.content:
Hello [i]Mictlan [/i]fans!

What character would you like to see represented in [i]Mictlan [/i]from one of the many [b]Mexican pre-Hispanic cultures[/b]?

Our intent is to give[b] visibility and representation [/b]in our game to the great civilizations that existed throughout Mexico.

In this concept art, you can see the [b]Pentamuti[/b], or Purépecha or Tarascan priest, the person responsible for watching over the Cuerauaperi cult, mother goddess of the Purepecha culture.

As you can see, the character wears a richly decorated [i]xicolli [/i]or nightgown, accompanied by [b]ornaments [/b]of bronze and gold, since the Purépecha were renowned [b]goldsmiths [/b]who worked metals, especially copper, and their knowledge gave them an advantage over their Mexican rivals. This character also wears a [b]funerary mask[/b], possibly for a mortuary ritual. Hanging behind him, a huge dry gourd that serves either to store water for libations in honor of the gods, or as a deposit of medicinal powders used to heal the sick.

What do you think?

notes.title: The fire that destroyed the temple
notes.content:
​For the Aztecs, [b]omens [/b]were important events that predicted [b]danger of the empire[/b].  

As a matter of fact, in the years before the [b]arrival of the Spanish[/b], there were a series of events which the Aztecs interpreted as [b]bad omens[/b].

​The third omen was when a[b] bolt of lightning[/b] hit the temple of the god of fire, Xiuhtecuhtli. Sahagun sources indicate that the bolt of lighting had [b]no thunder nor sound[/b] associated with it. The inexorable fire and flames overcame the temple and [b]destroyed it[/b].

This temple, historically described as a thatched roof structure, has been [b]reimagined[/b] by our extremely talented collaborator @kuzeh75. Taking elements such as the statues of Huehuetéotl, Xiuhcoatl, and a pyramidal structure with a wooden shrine covered by stucco, he brought to life a [b]unique interpretation[/b] of the third dire omen.

What do you think of the WIP of the Temple of Xiuhtecuhtli? Do you like it? 

What do you think about the omens? [b]Let us know in the comments[/b]!

notes.title: Terrible omens
notes.content:
Omens and divinations were part of[b] Mexica mysticism[/b], so it is not surprising that the wise men and Tlatoanis interpreted the strange [b]signs [/b]that appeared before the conquest of Tenochtitlán as signals sent by the gods, a warning about [b]the end of an era[/b] and of the cyclical battle between the gods.

The passing of a [b]comet[/b], the [b]lightning [/b]strike at the Xiuhtecuhtli temple, the sudden [b]fire [/b]of the Templo Mayor, the appearance of a "[b]weeping woman[/b]" in the streets, crying out in the night, warning her "children" to flee.

The final omen was when a [b]two-headed monster[/b] was discovered in the city of Tenochtitlan.

All the omens revealed the [b]uncertainty of the future [/b]of the Mexica nation in the face of fate. 
[i]A grim future indeed.[/i]

notes.title: Yohualtepoztli
notes.content:
This is the story of one of the most [b]frightening beings[/b] in Tenochtitlan: it exists to [b]torment nocturnal travelers[/b], a beast that appears to the ones who dare to walk alone at night. 

A humanoid creature, that has no head. Its chest is wide open: a revolting, bloody cavity displaying its [b]heart[/b], trapped in the ribcage.

[i]Thud. Thud. Thud. [/i]
You'll hear it coming, like an [b]axe [/b]being driven into wood.
That's where the name of the [b]Yohualtepoztli [/b]comes from: [i]yohualli[/i], “night”, and [i]tepoztli[/i], “axe”.

Faced with this creature, there's little you can to: either [b]flee [/b]or try to [b]rip its heart off its chest[/b].

So, [i]what will it be?[/i]
