notes.title: The power of Unreal Engine 5
notes.content:
A couple months back, we upgraded to [b]Unreal Engine 5[/b], which gives us the possibility of working with [b]photogrammetric scanned assets[/b], and keeping the same level of graphics. Millions of un-optimized polygons are the[b] dream [/b]that any developer could ever dream of.

To be able to deliver a world using the latest technology in terms of graphics, our awesome team is working on the details of the [b]micro-world[/b] inside the videogame.

We are working with many groups in Mexico to [b]scan jungles[/b], [b]mountains[/b], [b]plants[/b], [b]rocks[/b], and even the smallest details in the environment, to give that touch of [b]realism [/b]never seen before in LATAM.
Our dream is to create the first open-world videogame based on [b]pre-Hispanic cultures[/b]. To accomplish this, we are learning, investigating and researching to [b]make this dream a reality[/b].

notes.title: Design study of a young Mexica priest
notes.content:
Did you know that Mexica priests used to wear [b]dreadlocks [/b]created with the blood of [b]self-sacrifice[/b] to commemorate the deities of the underworld?

We talked about priests with dreadlocks in [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/4625732561661882295]this post[/url] and today we're showing you this new design study of a [b]young mexica priest[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/abcb97be2a58b7c7258a8816314265dbcbb3cc2d.png[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/7676ff68733a172e22056644f4feba59b284c225.png[/img]

The introduction to [b]Mexican priesthood[/b] was a task that began from an early age, when children of [b]nobles and commoners [/b]were both eligible, without distinction of social stratum. They were instructed in the rigid [b]Mexican morality[/b] in addition to the worship of their gods, where they performed various tasks like cleaning, preparation of offerings and study of doctrine.

The majority of the novices would return to their usual activities after a period of time, returning to their original ranks in the social scale, but others, [b]the most pious and advantaged[/b] under the gaze of their mentors, would become priests, climbing the social pyramid, either as [b]counselors or generals [/b]of the priestly military regiment of the empire.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/be86cf7d282fe3d7e653cdc61f47431a83f27e9d.png[/img]

notes.title: Remembering Miss María
notes.content:
Dear [i]Mictlan [/i]fans. 

Today we want to[b] pay our respects[/b], showing a render to remember [b]Miss María[/b], a woman full of love, kindness and joy, who recently passed away. She was a beloved member of the [b]Mexican community in Japan[/b] and a [b]spiritual mother [/b]to many compatriots living abroad. 

Being in life a true master in gastronomy and guardian of the Mexican traditions, we decided to make her character a [b]Mexica cook[/b] with red achiote hair and blooming flowers with four petals on her [i]huipil[/i]. She will be the one bringing food to those who are starving, feeding both their stomachs and their [b]souls [/b]with her indomitable spirit.
 
With the passing of Miss María, a [b]great friend of our director [/b]Guillermo Alarcon, we feel like the world has lost a bit of its beauty, but we also know that someday, beyond the Apanohuaina,[b] we'll see each other again[/b].

notes.title: Sisimite #2
notes.content:
Remember the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2992060508099033138]concept art[/url] we shared about the [b]sisimite[/b]? 

A truly savage creature which is slowly coming to life thanks to the work of our incredible art team: 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/b7e61c153fb3b0a52b72884b2db4bd477a41faa8.jpg[/img]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/594fa235dc7a72eac5591bc8b3e04616c61f717a.jpg[/img]

This ape-like creature, with disturbing backward-facing feet, is mistakenly known by some people as the “[b]Mexican Bigfoot[/b]”. It's actually a creature from the legends in Honduras, Guatemala, Belize, Nicaragua and El Salvador.

It dwells in hidden caves in the Central American [b]high mountains[/b], and all the stories about it describe the sisimite as a [b]morally ambivalent creature[/b]. On one hand, it is an[b] herbivore [/b]that feeds on wild fruits and protects small animals from human hunters and fishermen. On the other hand, it captures women and takes them to the caves, forcing them to give birth to ape-men.

Despite its scary appearance, you'll be glad to know that the sisimite has[b] two elemental weaknesses[/b]: water and fire. 

[b]Picture this[/b]: you are backtracking a set of four-fingered footprints leading to the mountain; there, you find the sisimite’s lair, and you bravely chase it away (or even defeat it!) exploiting its elemental weaknesses, finally reaching your objective: a cave that will grant you access to the underworld.

This is just an idea, but… how do you imagine your own encounter with the sisimite in the open world of [i]Mictlan[/i]?

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/be86cf7d282fe3d7e653cdc61f47431a83f27e9d.png[/img]

Legends, myths, facts, history: [i]Mictlan [/i]has it all! We're aiming at including in our game the most incredible stories, and we will continue updating you with news, concept arts, sneak&peeks of our creative process, so make sure to follow us on our social media channels to stay updated!

notes.content:
Today we want to share more about the process we go through to capture the photorealism of [i]Mictlan[/i]'s characters.

We're investing our time and resources to recreate the [b]original cultures of Mexico[/b]. During our travels, we met Milpa Alta, a [b]descendant of the Nahua kinfolks[/b], who spoke to us in his native language about the [b]old days[/b] of his life.

Using the digital photogrammetry technique, we were able to define the dimensions and location of each of the [b]details of his facial features[/b]. 

He asked to be a [b][url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/4509778749607407868]pochteca [/url][/b](merchant) in the game, therefore, in the digital transition, we decided to make him [b]a little younger[/b] - since he is actually 94 years old - so that his character was [b]consistent [/b]with his in-game role in [i]Mictlan[/i].

notes.title: How we're including the Nahual in Mictlan
notes.content:
The legends of the [b]nahual [/b]in Mexico have deep roots in [b]magical events [/b]and folklore.

These mythical beings are [b]guardian-spirits[/b] intimately linked to their humans, who feel a mix of fear and admiration before their extraordinary powers.

Nahual is believed to reside in an [b]animal[/b], such as a deer, jaguar, or bird. Others believe the nagual is the animal into which certain [b]powerful men[/b] can transform themselves, acquiring the animal's unbelievable skills (we've talked about the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3005569403402945591]Nahual kids[/url] before).

🔥 In [i]Mictlan[/i], we've been working really hard to design a [b]special dynamic[/b] in which the characters can contact their nahual (spiritual companion) by two different methods.

🐆 They can make an [b]invocation[/b] to let these creatures manifest themselves in the physical world as [b]allies [/b]in battle and as an aid to discover [b]secret locations[/b]. 

🐦 We also thought about the idea of letting the player [b]become one with their nahual[/b], transforming themself into powerful animals with a [b]unique set of abilities[/b].

[h3]What do you think? Would you call you nahual in the game? Would you prefer transforming yourself into one? 

We would really appreciate [b]your feedback[/b] about this. 
Let us know what you think in the comments![/h3]

notes.title: Huehuecoyotl #2
notes.content:
Its [b]howls [/b]have been deaf for centuries, its songs and music have been nothing more than just [b]empty echoes[/b], desperate to be heard [b]once more[/b].

In [i]Mictlan [/i]you will be able to hear the nocturnal howls of [b]Huehuecoyotl[/b], the god of the arts, music and dance. ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3029213935088016668]We showed you the concept art of this character in this post![/url])

Its name is derived from Nahuatl and means "[b]Old Coyote[/b]", as it is represented as a virile man with the face of a coyote. A warrior and [b]sower of discord[/b] among men, Huehuecoyotl was also described as a [i]malsin [/i](that is, a gossiper).

Huehuecoyotl is considered a god of [b]good luck[/b], based on the fact that he is the one who represents the limit between good and evil. He [b]balances [/b]the old and the new, the mundane and the spiritual, the youth and the old, the male and the female, since he has the ability to [b]change gende[/b]r. It is also characterized by [b]lust[/b] and [b]carnal desire[/b], giving way to the erotic dimension of the ancient Mexicas.

notes.title: Huehuetéotl #2
notes.content:
The figure and insignia of [b]Huehuetéotl-Xiuhtecuhtli[/b], the ancient Mesoamerican [b]god of fire and time[/b] ([i]xiuhitl [/i]in Nahuatl, the language of the Aztecs, meant both 'turquoise' and 'year'), appeared long before the Mexica integrated it into their pantheon as a representation of the [b]first cosmic force[/b] that sustains and gives birth to the other gods.

Huehuetéotl ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2992060508106410276]we showed the first concept art pieces here[/url]) is represented as an old man carrying a [b]huge brazier[/b]. One of his emblems was the cross, which placed him at the [b]center of the four directions[/b] of the universe. 

Every 52 years, in the [i]izcalli [/i](home) month, the [b]New Fire ritual [/b]was celebrated, making an effigy of him with a turquoise mask, while the fire in his temple was renewed to distribute it in each home of Tenochtitlan: it was a symbol of the[b] cyclical death and resurrection of life[/b]. It was by far [b]the most important event[/b] in the religious calendar: if the ceremony failed, then the Aztec civilization [b]would end[/b].

This is just a #WIP, a preview of the creative work we do to bring [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i] to life, making images as detailed as possible to be able to convey the [b]powerful symbolism[/b] behind each and every character.

notes.title: Pochteca
notes.content:
This is a sample of the modeling work of a [b]merchant [/b]or [b][i]Pochteca[/i][/b], who were the main traders, importers and exporters of goods in the [b]Aztec Empire[/b].

Although the term [i]Pochteca [/i]is used to refer to any merchant, for the ancient Pochtecas this profession was divided into four classifications:

The [b]Tlachiuhqui[/b]: They were producers who manufactured everything they sold. This work was carried out across the entire Aztec territory.

The [b]Tlanamacac[/b]: They were dedicated to buying and selling.

The [b]Tlanecuilos[/b]: They were retailers, and those who obtained the most profits from commerce.

The [b]Oztomecatl[/b]: They were importers, who usually traveled and carried out important expeditions to the corners of the empire.

The [i]Pochtecas [/i]will be the vendors that will [b]sell you weapons[/b], [b]accessories [/b]and [b]medicinal plants[/b], and they will help you create[b] your own items[/b].

notes.title: Tlacamexquimilli
notes.content:
[b]Tlacamexquimilli[/b]: Bulk of Ashes

When a Mexica died from natural causes, the [b]body was wrapped[/b] in a fetal position inside of a rucksack, along with different elements that they would need in [b]their journey to [i]Mictlan[/i][/b].

But, apparently, some of them [b]did not make it [/b]to that point, and they would appear as “[b]spirits[/b]”, roaming the roads and streets. They would take the form of a [b]bulk of ashes[/b] or of a [b]shrouded corpse[/b], they could have many heads or legs, or resemble a[b] shapeless mass[/b], full of eyes and sharp teeth, wandering in the night to scare the living.

On many occasions, people would [b]die from fear[/b] caused by ghosts.

Some said that this was actually [b]a trick from Tezcatlipoc[/b]a to test the warriors. If they were brave, he would reward them with a [b]symbolic gift[/b]; but if they were cowards, they would[b] surely die[/b] on the battlefield or from diseases. 

These are some pieces from our designers, they still are in progress [b]#WIP[/b].

[h3]Which one do you find more terrifying?[/h3]

notes.title: Cuauhtemoc
notes.content:
[b]Cuauhtemoc[/b], the [i]descending eagle[/i]. 

What a prophetic name for such a [b]heroic and tragic figure[/b] in the history of Mexico! 

He did not inherit a flourishing empire like Moctezuma II, but one fragmented by the European invasion. As the [b]military leader[/b] of the Mexica, he fought for the survival of his people, [b]fortifying the city of Tenochtitlan[/b] and preparing his people for a war without truce, a war that would culminate in the [b]destruction[/b] of one of the most impressive cities in pre-Hispanic America.

How to do justice to [b]such a remarkable figure[/b]? 

In the [b]concept art[/b] we created, we decided not to show Cuauhtemoc in the typical attire of his rank, but fighting like a [i]macehual [/i]warrior. Of course, he's wearing some emblems that represent the [b]important position[/b] he held, but the general [b]modest attire[/b] represents the lack of resources and the [b]suffering of the besieged city[/b] that he tried to defend so bravely. At the same time, Cuauhtemoc's [b]defiant pose[/b] reminds us of his legendary [b]stoicism and courage[/b], ready to sacrifice himself for his people, to safeguard a world that was doomed, but that he refused to let go without a [b]fierce fight[/b]. 

[h3]Which one of these variations is your favorite? 

Let us know in the comments![/h3]

notes.title: Tarascan warrior
notes.content:
Hello, dear followers of [i]Mictlan[/i]! 

Today we want to show you some concept art pieces related to the [b]Michoacan region[/b].

The West of Mexico is still an [b]enigma [/b]for archaeologists: the migratory flow of the region has not yet been precisely determined, but the archaeological evidence discovered so far speaks of contacts from time immemorial with the [b]Andean area[/b], reflected in the ceramics and lithics found in the Tombs of the [b]Colima region[/b].

That is why, in order to represent the [b]Tarascan warrior[/b], we took into account the relations of [b]Michoacan [/b](a document created by the Franciscan Fray Jerónimo de Alcalá), which illustrates in details the customs and beliefs of the people of the Michoacan region, as well as their history during the [b]Spanish conquest[/b].

We also refer to some [b]sculptures [/b]found in the Colima region that represent warriors from that area, who fought against the Tarascans and who, in turn, served as their mercenaries in the so-called "[b]saltpeter wars[/b]"

This WIP was made by [b]MarioRicoArt[/b]. If you want to know more about his work, visit his [url=https://www.marioricoart.com/]website[/url].

notes.title: Palace of Moctezuma II
notes.content:
In this new piece of concept art, we want to show the facade of the [b]palace of Moctezuma II[/b], an architectural complex that the Tlatoani ordered to be built as a residence and seat of[b] government of the city of Tenochtitlan[/b], thus replacing the old palace of Axayacatl and thereby giving life to a glorious government that would [b]end abruptly[/b] after the arrival of the Spanish conquistadores to Mesoamerica.

The chroniclers of the time, such as Bernal Díaz del Castillo's, described in detail the palace of Moctezuma II. In the words of [b]Hernán Cortés[/b]:

[quote]He had his lodgings within the city, such and so wonderful, that it seemed almost impossible to tell the goodness and greatness of them. Therefore, I won’t be able to express something about them, more than that in Spain there is no one similar.[/quote]

Given that the [b]archaeological evidence is scarce[/b] since the Moctezuma palace lies buried in the metropolitan area of ​​Mexico City and that the descriptions of [b]Fray Bernardino de Sahagún [/b]would be written several years after the destruction of Tenochtitlan, we took [b]some artistic liberties[/b], supported by Mexica architectural remains of the time, and speculation of how the great palace of Moctezuma II could have been.

[h3]What do you think of this WIP?[/h3]

notes.title: Tetzcotzinco
notes.content:
On the slopes of the [b]Tetzcotzinco hill[/b], there are the impressive archaeological remains of a recreational space that the [b]emperor poet Netzahualcóyotl[/b] had created for resting, meditation and pleasure.

It is said that the design was designed by the ruler himself, it included palaces, altars and temples, pools for bathing and a [b]complex system of aqueducts [/b]that brought water from the foothills of the Sierra Nevada, more than 6 km away. The aqueduct is considered [b]one of the most important hydraulic works [/b]from pre-Hispanic times.

The site's historical value lies in its hydraulic system but also in its [b]vast gardens[/b], with stairways, channels and sculptures. It was a center for astronomical observations and for performing of social, political and religious rituals.

The so-called [b]Bath of Xochitl[/b] stands out, it is believed to have belonged to the wife of the Poet King. It has a circular font that is accessible by a staircase, with vestiges of the sculptures of frogs still preserved.

notes.title: The Great Tenochtitlan #2
notes.content:
Here is another update about the [b]biggest and most advanced city[/b] in the 15th century. That's right, we're talking about [b]Tenochtitlan[/b]!

If you missed the [b]previous posts[/b] about it, here they are: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2969545680704939381]#1[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2969546585728032228]#2[/url] 

The city had a wonderful and well-planned[b] tangle of streets[/b] and canals that gave it a mystical (and functional) look.
The streets of Tenochtitlan had sidewalks of rammed earth* for human transit, and some of them had adjacent [b]canals [/b]for the transit of canoes that transported and commercialized a lot of different products.

The first [b]main street[/b] (and the most used for commercial purposes) was [b]Tlalpan[/b], built by the Xochimilcas as an act of tribute to the Mexica; it started in Xochimilco and ended in Tenochtitlan.

[h3]Become a [b]merchant [/b]in our game![/h3]

Each NPC will have a different[b] cinematic animation[/b] for their purchase sequences, making it [b]unique [/b]in the entire open world of [i]Mictlan[/i], something never seen before in Latin America.

Remember that the [b]Pochtecas [/b]traded with different types of merchandise and materials.

notes.title: The Great Tenochtitlan
notes.content:
Today we present to you the [b]incredible work[/b] that our 3D artists, lead by our talented artist [b]Josharts3d[/b], are doing in recreating the[b] Great Tenochtitlan[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/08d9295b1a766b1abe33ebdbd5103a26464d8508.jpg[/img]

The faithful recreation of this place will be of utmost importance since Tenochtitlan was [b]the center of the Aztec universe[/b].
Just in its [b]Great Plaza [/b]were over [b]80 buildings[/b] between temples, altars, warrior rooms, the Calmecac, palaces and other structures.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/518e3b64da03b4d3bdef8b16841673841c86987c.jpg[/img]

[b]The residences of the nobility [/b]and [b]administrative buildings[/b] were organized around squares or open spaces, connected by roads and canals. Artisans and peasants organized themselves into neighborhoods or [i]Calpullis[/i]. According to Roger Bartra's calculations, the population was around [b]700,000[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/3b3fd5913e057e436637bb4397c5d8e2be14aad5.jpg[/img]

This data [b]is all the more impressive[/b] when thinking about the fact that the city was founded on an [b]islet [/b]in Lake Texcoco, and that the Aztecs built [b]artificial islands [/b]as villages that, as the settlement expanded, were eventually [b]integrated into the city[/b].

notes.title: The coastal city of Tulum
notes.content:
Today we proudly present to you some images (WIP) of a level dedicated to one of the [b]most powerful coastal settlements[/b] in the late Postclassic period, the great walled city of the Caribbean: [b]Tulum[/b]. 

Known in the 16th century as [b]Zamá [/b](which means “[b]dawn[/b]”), the site of Tulum was one of the most important centers of exchange on the sea that connected the Gulf of Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. It was a [b]seaport[/b], trading mainly in turquoise and jade.

The hard work of our [b]3D department[/b] resulted in an artistic reconstruction of the main architectural complexes in the city, so that you can [b]explore the castle[/b], the Temple of Frescoes, the Temple of the Falling God, and the palaces and altars all around the [b]archaeological zone[/b]. 

[i]Note[/i]:
This render is not the final version, the finished version of Tulum can be admired at the[b] end of 2024 - 2025[/b], when we plan to release our game.

With this artistic interpretation we want to bring Tulum to its old days of glory, so… [b]What do you think? [/b]Would you like to see Tulum in the world of [i]Mictlan[/i]? 
[b]Let us know in the comments[/b]!

notes.title: A bunch of severed heads
notes.content:
[quote]No other body part represents a person like the head. It is the center of vision, language and thought.[/quote]

In multiple cultures, the display of [b]human heads[/b] was a common practice. 
In the Great Tenochtitlan, the [i]Tzompantli [/i]was the altar where the severed heads of the captives were impaled, in order to honor the gods.

According to the archaeologist[b] Eduardo Matos Moctezuma[/b]: “Templo Mayor was the great Mexica ceremonial center, and it was built on two axes: that of death, represented by Hutizilopochtli, and that of life, represented by the god Tlaloc… because the Mexica worshiped life through death”.

In Tenochtitlan there were [b]seven [/b]of these constructions, associated with seven different gods; and they were built from a stone platform, on which a scaffold with thin wooden rods was raised, and it was used to [b]pierce the human skulls[/b] through their temples.

What do you think? Would you like to see such bloody scenes (the decapitation and impalement of the heads) in our video game? 
[b]Let us know in the comments![/b]

notes.title: The challenges behind Mictlan
notes.content:
It is not easy to develop a video game such as [i]Mictlan[/i]. 

The[b] level of hyperrealism [/b]that we have set to achieve takes a lot of work and a talented team. It all starts with [b]historiographic research[/b], then our artists create[b] concept art[/b], which finally reaches the capable hands of our [b]3D modelers[/b]. They are the ones who, at a high level of [b]digital craftsmanship[/b], build everything that you will admire in [i]Mictlan[/i]: buildings, diverse biomes, weapons, animals and, of course, characters.

We are an [b]independent studio[/b], so we have to use a public software. Fortunately, [b]Unreal Engine [/b]gives our artists the possibility to accomplish amazing things and achieve a level of detail and quality that we plan to offer to our players.

But it is not just about the tools: it is the talent and the [b]heart of our team[/b], mostly Mexican people, which makes [i]Mictlan [/i]a project that will surpass everything that has been done among video games in Latin America to this day. 

[b]Your help[/b], the help of [b]our community[/b] is fundamental to achieve this dream and shift the paradigms for a lot of Latin American creators.

notes.title: Tamoanchan
notes.content:
[b]Tamoanchan [/b]is a mythical place where a broken, flowering [b]tree [/b]grows. A divine force irradiates from it with so much power, that not only it is capable of [b]giving life[/b], but also of regenerating life, bringing the dead back to life.

It is said that the broken tree representing Temoanchan emerges from [b]a place where the gods were born[/b] and it then grew over the 7 caves (Chicomoztoc), from where the Aztecs separated from 6 other tribes (with which they shared Nahua lineage) and from where they left, guided by their god Huitzilopochtli.

Temoanchan is the place where Quetzalcoatl revived the [b]bones of the ancestors[/b] to resurrect humanity, creating the first man and woman that would live in the World of the Fifth Sun. There, corn sprouted for the first time, and there began the pilgrimage of the Aztecs towards their destiny.

According to some experts*, Tamoanchan represents a [b]mythical region[/b] where gods, human beings, creatures, food, plants and nations [b]originated[/b]… 

In the image you can see one of the scenes of the [b]animated short[/b] that we are working on.

Take a look at these three sneak peek we already shared, to have an idea of what we're working on!

notes.title: Guillermo Alarcón's photographs
notes.content:
Today we want to take the chance to present the work of our Creative Director, [b]Guillermo Alarcón[/b], whose [b]photographs [/b]are a precious memento of his travels around the world.

[quote]The search for my roots and cultural identity is what sparked my passion for Mesoamerica civilizations in the first place. Born in Mexico but raised in San Francisco, I have visited [b]97 countries in 9 years[/b]. My travels gave me the opportunity to explore archaeological sites around the world, dive deep into ancestral cultures, spirituality and shamanism, gaining an extensive knowledge of the Mexican culture. In 2012, I also had the opportunity to live in an [b]indigenous Mayan community[/b] near the Chichen Itza ruins. I learned about their lifestyle and traditions, explored the Yucatan jungle, built huts and collected plants. I learned a lot about myself and about the indigenous people’s rich cultural legacy. Although I now live in a very different jungle, the city of Tokyo, I still carry in my heart those life-changing experiences which have shaped the way I see the world and portray reality through my work. My background as a multimedia artist, photographer and filmmaker allowed me to lay the foundations to build [i]Mictlan[/i], [b]the game I have always wanted to create[/b] to convey my experiences and let other people appreciate the beauty of Mexican culture and myths.[/quote]

Guillermo decided to share his work with [i]Mictlan's [/i]fans in order to let others appreciate the beauty of some of the life-changing moments he has lived and also to be able to [b]support [/b]the development of the game, by selling his pictures. 

Available in [b]metal framing and acrylic emulsion,[/b] these high-quality images are printed on metal sheet through a special printing process that is exclusively used for museums and important galleries. 

You can find them in [i]Mictlan[/i]’s[b] official store[/b]:
https://store.mictlanthegame.com/

Furthermore, these photos and other official Mictlan merchandise will feature as [b]rewards [/b]in our [b]Kickstarter campaign[/b]. And, on top of that, some of these physical printings will come with an exclusive collectible [b]NFT[/b], which will digitally authenticate you as a unique owner of one of Guillermo Alarcón’s photographic artworks.

notes.title: Mexico-Tenochtitlan causeways
notes.content:
Greetings, dear [i]Mictlan [/i]fans!

Today, we will talk about the [b]Mexico-Tenochtitlan causeways[/b].

Roads, unlike the numerous canals that crossed the city, had been designed with the purpose of speeding up the[b] traffic of people[/b] inside and outside the city, as well as the [b]circulation of goods[/b] that could not travel by lake. These causeways had a [b]considerable length[/b], up to 20 meters, a [b]feat of engineering[/b] achieved in ancient Mexico.

There were [b]four main roads[/b] in the city. 
[i]Iztapalapa [/i]was the busiest; it faced south and connected the city with the towns of Coyoacan, Xochimilco and Chalco. [i]Tacuba [/i]led to the west. Towards the north, a minor one led to a canal named Tezontlali, which was connected to Tepeyac; and finally, [i]Tepeyac [/i] was connected to a large pier that gave access to the kingdom of Texcoco.

In [i]Mictlan[/i], we want [b]the players to travel[/b] these important routes and immerse themselves in the [b]daily life[/b] of this mythical city.

Note: This is not the final render, you will enjoy the finished version of Tenochtitlan at the end of 2024 - 2025

notes.title: Miquiztetl
notes.content:
The cruel [b]Miquiztetl[/b] was a deity from the underworld who tried to stop the dead from overcoming the trials of the nine regions. When people died, they had to travel for 4 years, before arriving to [i]Mictlán[/i].

A skillful warrior and twin sister of the [b]God of Dreams[/b], she attacked those who descended to the world of the dead and [b]terrified them[/b] with her fierce and skeletal body. She attacked with her weapons and made them fall into different [b]traps [/b]that the dead had to overcome, before going through the nine levels that blocked their access to [i]Mictlan[/i].

After a long journey through the underground regions, the dead had to rid of their [b]fears[/b], traps, and tricks of Miquiztetl, to prove that they were capable of freeing their [i]Tonalli [/i]([b]soul[/b]) from all the life burdens.

They finally arrived in front of the [b]lord and mistress of death[/b]: Mictlantecuhtli and Mictlancíhuatl, rulers of the underworld, who allowed the souls to leave behind all the pain that they had carried during their lives, in order to finally [b]rest in peace[/b].

notes.title: Beauty standards in the pre-Hispanic world
notes.content:
There were many beauty standards in the pre-Hispanic world, when the[b] cult of the body [/b]was central. 

As we've [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1411900/view/3026951542954716803]discussed before in this post[/url], the ancient populations considered the human body as a small representation of the cosmo and used the body as a "[b]canvas[/b]" to achieve the ideal beauty.  
They [b]altered [/b]their physical appearance in many ways, such as body paint, tattoos, jewelry: all of this represented an expression of [b]cultural identity[/b] and [b]social belonging[/b].

[b]Scarification [/b]was another method used by ancient civilizations to signify important events in one's life, as well as to symbolize differing class distinctions. This process consisted of multiple [b]skin perforations[/b], followed by stuffing the wound with some kind of irritating substance, such as small stones, dirt or ashes. This process led to several [b]scars [/b]with different textures, forming [b]complex patterns[/b].

The evidence these practices (tattooing, scarification, and body paint) among the Maya comes from [b]iconographic images[/b] such as pottery and murals, artifacts such as tools and vessels used for storing pigment and anthropomorphic sculptures.

notes.title: Amoxoaques: It's the details that matter
notes.content:
[b]Writing is power[/b]. 
In ancient times, written memories gave legitimacy to states, while the destruction of written texts would condemn some civilizations to oblivion.

The Olmecs were the [b]earliest known[/b] major Mesoamerican civilization. The Epi-Olmec culture (a successor culture to the Olmec) featured a full-fledged [b]writing system[/b] know as [b]Epi-Olmec script[/b].

Writing, especially in the earliest forms, was so important that we decided to show it in this concept art of the [b]Amoxoaque Tlaltecui[/b]: on its surface, you can see [b]glyphs [/b]from the Epi-Olmec writing. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/a06fd343706318d0e061e1482b0bf3a84853ef3a.jpg[/img]

We're also very proud to show you the [b]renders [/b]of our Amoxoaque, where you can see [b]all the details[/b] on their rough bark-like skin (you can also take a look at the [i]related previous posts[/i]: [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3016822062043677867]#1[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/4855419242356564479]#2[/url], [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3005569403402928230]#3[/url])

Being able to include these [b]mythical creatures[/b], these great sages from [b]cultures of pre-Hispanic Mexico[/b], makes us truly happy, excited and proud. 

We want to [b]revive ancient tales [/b]and great legends from our past and from our ancestors, and we're doing it by [b]thorough historical research[/b] and analysis, in order to bring you an amazing, original, [b]culturally rich game[/b]: [i]Mictlan[/i]!

notes.title: Teotihuacan
notes.content:
Among the archeological sites found in Mexico that are open to the public, [b]Teotihuacan [/b]is one of the most visited by tourists from all over the world, even more than Chichen Itza and Monte Alban. 

It is usual, among the people who visit Mexico City for their first time, to take some pictures at the top of the [b]Pyramid of the Sun[/b], as a token to remember the tiring trek up the dozens of very small and steep stairs, in order to “[b]recharge with positive energy[/b]”.

Although some of these popular beliefs derive from recent movements such as [i]the new age[/i], it is true that you can feel a [b]mystic and enigmatic presence[/b] when walking through the historical roads of the site, between the elite houses of the ancient Teotihuacan society. 

And it is not just us that perceive this mysterious feeling: half a millennium ago, the Mexica, trying to understand how such a [b]grand and majestic city [/b]ended up being abandoned, decided to entitle it as “the [b]City of Gods[/b]” and to establish it as the origin of the[b] Fifth Sun[/b], so that it effectively became the birthplace of the last era of the world as we know it.

Beyond myths and tales, it is actually proven that, in order to build it, its architects observed the position of the [b]celestial bodies[/b], taking into consideration the calendar in order to mark ritual and agricultural seasons. 

Besides, we can’t overlook the strange[b] coincidences[/b] with the construction of the Pyramid of Cheops in Egypt: they have [b]striking architectural similarities[/b], even if built by two completely unrelated societies.

What do you expect to find when you play [i]Mictlan [/i]and go visit Teotihuacan? 
Do you have any pictures of you in this enigmatic city? Share in the comments [url=https://www.facebook.com/mictlanthegame/posts/291813155977356]to this post[/url]!

notes.title: Macehuales
notes.content:
Greetings, [i]Mictlan [/i]community!

Today we will talk about the [i]macehuales[/i]: the base of Mexica society.

Aztec society was strictly [b]hierarchical[/b], divided into clearly defined classes so that individuals would have remained in the social group of their immediate family throughout their lives.

The macehuales were by far the[b] largest section [/b]of Aztec society, they were the ones who cultivated the land, those who paid the taxes and reinforced the size of the army.

Aside from the commoner-warriors, the macehual class was further [b]differentiated [/b]into class levels. Certain occupations were considered to have [b]higher prestige[/b] than others (such as merchants, goldsmiths, and featherworkers). In general, compared with rural farming, all [b]urban [/b]occupations were assigned higher status.

Macehuales had a [b]hard [/b]and [b]humble life[/b], always working long hours to get by.

In this concept art you can see a young macehual with a [i]mecapal[/i], a container which was widely used in pre-Hispanic times to transport [b]all kinds of goods[/b], goods which would surely be exchanged in the [i]tianguis[/i] (open-air market) of Tlatelolco.
We also drew the young boy with a [i]coa[/i], a [b]digging tool [/b]that was used for farming and at the time, also as an improvised weapon.

notes.title: Tortilleras
notes.content:
Mighty gods, supernatural creatures, ancient legends... Do you know what else played a [b]central part[/b] in Aztec mythology?

[b]Corn[/b].

That's right, corn was the [b]most important staple[/b] at that time, the most precious [b]gift [/b]the gods gifted their children with, the [b]fundamental crop [/b]which shaped all the societies developing in[b] ancient Mexico[/b].

No one knows who was the first tortilla maker, but certainly, [b]tortilleras[/b] are such important figures, we absolutely had to include them in [i]Mictlan[/i].

As references, we used images of the goddess [b]Chicomecoatl[/b], also taking into consideration the ritual decorations that tortilleras wear in [b]Otomi festivities[/b], from the Tlaxcala region.

notes.title: Tlatoani #2
notes.content:
Differently from the [i]huey tlatoani[/i], the “Lord of lords” who ruled over all of the other [i]altepetls [/i]in the Aztec Empire, with the title of "Great Speaker", the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3005569403402948455]tlatoani [/url]focused more on the needs of their region. 

They had the [b]most important[/b] position in Tenochtitlan, in terms of political hierarchy. The only people who were able to become a tlatoani were the [b]descendants [/b]of the first tlatoani. 
Only those deemed worthy of this title were chosen to inherit the throne. 
A [b]Council [/b]of royal members helped to make this decision by choosing those who had the necessary attributes to reign with [b]wisdom [/b]and [b]efficiency[/b].

The tlacochcaltl was one of the most prominent positions in the Tenochtitlan hierarchy, held by men of the [b]royal [/b]lineage. When the [b]sovereign [/b]died, the new one was chosen among them, 

The cape that they wore was called[i] tucucizyo tilmatli[/i].

What do you think of this character?
Let us know in the comments!

notes.title: What if the legends were true...?
notes.content:
You are walking in the middle of a [b]forest[/b], making your way through the thick foliage. 
You hear a distant [b]noise [/b]echoing through the trees. 
You hear it again. It's getting [b]closer[/b], it's getting [b]louder[/b]. 
A dark shadow suddenly moves across the sky, hovering over you. 
You look up, paralyzed by [b]shock [/b]and [b]fear[/b]: standing on the ground, as [b]tall [/b]as the trees stretching up to the sky, you see an [b]enormous human figure[/b] looking down at you. 

The legends are true: you're looking at a [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/partnerevents/preview/3046099263127217385]Quinametli[/url].

The Quinametzin are often mentioned in Aztec and [b]Mesoamerican mythology[/b] and in Spanish chronicles. 
These mysterious figures stood over 10 feet tall and weighed around 600 pounds. They lived in a time known as the [b]Era of the Fourth Sun[/b] and it is believed that it was them who built the [b]pyramids [/b]of Teotihuacán and the Great Pyramid of Cholula.

In these pictures, you can see the concept behind one of our [b]cinematic sequences [/b]that you will find in [i]Mictlan[/i].

notes.title: Some pictures from our 3D rendering process
notes.content:
Today we want to show you some pictures from the [b]3D rendering process[/b] behind the creation of our characters. This is a complex and very long process when creating 3D images, because it's the phase when the computer puts together [b]all the data[/b] to generate the character that, later on, you’ll be controlling and interacting with when playing [i]Mictlan[/i].

It is [b]fascinating [/b]thinking that, in reality, everything we see on the screen is actually a compound of ‘zeroes’ and ‘ones’. A [b]series of numbers [/b]that, through the hard work of our designers and artists, take shape and transform into something almost [b]tangible[/b], allowing us to discover exciting new worlds.

What do you think? 
Leave us your comments and suggestions, because they constantly help us to improve!

notes.title: Huitzilopochtli
notes.content:
[b]Huitzilopochtli[/b], the god of war and of the sun, representing the mythical battle of [b]light against the darkness[/b]. A mighty and powerful god, whose strength derives from the [b]vital force[/b] of those who sacrificed themselves to him, from the [b]blood of the hearts[/b] that were offered to him.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/6cef8e62da38c6b013f44b233c1a74d7c72ce787.jpg[/img]

Huitzilopochtli is the one who guided the [b]long migration[/b] the Aztecs undertook from Aztlan, their traditional home, to the Valley of Mexico, where they founded the [b]Great Tenochtitlan[/b]. 

In these pictures, we want to show you one of the first versions of the Aztec god we created for [i]Micltan[/i]. We took the liberty of mixing the [b]historical [/b]codices with a [b]fantasy [/b]look suitable to represent this powerful figure. 

Although this is not the final version of the character, we wanted to present its render in real-time to give you an idea of our work.

notes.content:
Today we want to show you the concept art of [b]Itzpapalotl[/b], goddess of war, patroness of death, and councilor of the [i]Temoanchan Paradise[/i] (a mythical and earthly paradise).

The legend says that when Iztpapalotl was sent to Earth, falling from heaven, she wore an [b]invisible cloak [/b]so that no one could see her, giving her the power of [b]invisibility[/b].

 The [b]fearsome skeletal warrior goddess[/b] uses white makeup and different colors, and her chest pectoral represents [b]power [/b]and [b]fire[/b].

Itzpapalotl appears with [b]butterfly [/b]or [b]eagle [/b]attributes. In our concept art, her hands and feet are replaced by jaguar claws, this makes her a Tzitzimitl “a mythical terrible being”.

notes.title: Atlatl
notes.content:
Commonly known as a spear-thrower, the [b]Atlatl [/b]is, without a doubt, a [b]deadly weapon[/b]. 

This powerful weapon allowed warriors to throw spears from a great distance with deadly [b]force and speed[/b], easily piercing through any armor or enemy.

The weapon has an elongated body that ends in a [b]hook [/b]where the darts are placed, and it also possesses a handle with two perforations for a strong finger [b]grip[/b]. 
Capable of reaching a speed of[b] 130 km/h [/b](80 mph), [b]darts [/b]made of wood, flint, teeth, bone or obsidian. They were able to pierce the flesh and incapacitate an enemy [b]within seconds[/b]. 

In Mesoamerica, the Atlatl earned its fair place as a symbol of[b] war[/b], [b]power [/b]and [b]greatness[/b]. 
It became a must during the classic era wars. It was so important that in the temple of Jaguars, in Chichen Itza, almost [b]180 different soldiers [/b]were represented holding this particular weapon. 

[h3]Will you use the Atlatl in Mictlan? Or do you prefer melee weapons? 
Let us know in the comments! [/h3]

notes.title: Huehueteotl
notes.content:
[b]Huehueteotl[/b], which means "old god", is the[b] god of fire[/b]. A sage lord, the creator of all life, whose knowledge is as old as the world itself.

In Mesoamerican mythology, the [b]fundamental element of fire [/b]was thought to be present in the entire universe and wherever there was fire, so too was Huehueteotl.

The god of fire appears in various representations, one of which depicts him as a decrepit [b]old man[/b] with a stooped back, carrying an enormous, flaming [b]brazier [/b]on his head.

Sahagún describes him as a deity to be [b]feared [/b]and [b]loved[/b]. Fire can destroy everything, but it also provides light and heat to the people.

We decided to take into account all these elements to create this important character, as you can see from the pictures below.

notes.title: Member of the Nobility
notes.content:
[i]Niltze[/i], Mictlaners!
(Niltze means “hello” in náhuatl, the ancient Mexica language).

As you know, we are constantly creating[b] new characters[/b] that will populate the vast open world of [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i]. Today we want to show you a member of the [b]nobility[/b]. 

The high-class society generally lived in the royal palaces, helping in the temples or working as [b]advisors [/b]on politics and military matters for the [i]Tlatoani[/i]. They also worked as [b]judges [/b]and collected taxes, making sure to prevent fights and disputes in markets.

Some members of the nobility also assisted the priests in the [i]calmecac [/i](a school for the sons of Aztec nobility) teaching to children. Others, who were [b]war veterans[/b], helped train the new warriors in the [i]telpochcalli[/i] (where Aztec youth were educated, from age 15, to serve their community and for war).

The mexica society was very [b]advanced [/b]for its time, that's why we want to portray the cultural features of that society and of the people who lived in ancient Mexico, hoping to bring some aspects of the [b]Mexican culture[/b] to a wider audience.

notes.title: Spanish Soldiers
notes.content:
It is a [b]popular myth[/b] that the military efforts made by the Conquistadores were led by professional armies financed entirely by the Spanish crown while, actually, the exploration and conquest were carried out by [b]companies [/b]that were always [b]private [/b]in nature, which had to have the consent of the Crown.

in this concept art we show a few [b]Castilian warriors[/b], who stand out for their clothing and weapons; it is a very basic attire, since they only had the necessary equipment for a [b]hand-to-hand confrontation[/b]: a metal breatplate, a leather gown, which at the time were replaced by the padded armor known as [i]Ichcahuipilli[/i], since it was much more comfortable and protected the soldiers from arrows more efficiently.

During our studies, we realized that the morion helmet was not used by the Castilians in their initial expeditions to the Mexican territory, so we proceeded to study other styles of helmet used during the war; we also added the [b]adarga shield[/b], widely used in the Iberian Peninsula due to influence of the Berber people during the Caliphate period, until the Reconquest, and its use is documented in in documents such as the [i]Lienzo de Tlaxcala[/i].

notes.title: Nahual Kids #2
notes.content:
According to the different traditions of Mesoamerican cultures, it is believed that the first creature to cross over the ashes spread before a newborn baby becomes that child’s [b]nahual[/b], a [b]guardian spirit[/b]. 

Every newborn has their own personal guardian, depending on their day of birth. A spirit that watches over them and [b]protects them[/b]. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/4b82f147c64c048e6df99f5120982c0d7f12bad5.jpg[/img]

Kids can acquire [b]gifts [/b]and [b]special powers[/b] from their nahual, which can take the form of [b]various animals[/b] such as a jaguar, an eagle, a deer, or a snake (among others). 

The gifts can be granted but also removed and, if not handled well, they can [b]take hold of the will [/b]of a young person in the teenage years. That's why every Nagual kid has to learn to control and master their powers otherwise their entire existence is on the line.

In [i]Mictlan[/i], you will encounter these characters who can become your [b]greatest allies[/b]... or your [b]worst nightmare[/b].

notes.title: Huehuecoyotl
notes.content:
The Aztec god of poetry, music, dance, and mischief: [b]Huehuecoyotl[/b], the "Old Coyote", enters the pantheon of [i]Mictlan[/i]'s gods.

This very [b]unique-looking god[/b] is usually represented wearing garments made of "olive" shells and copper bells on arms and legs, which are associated with wind and music. He also has golden beads that fall from his hand as pictured in [i]Codex Borgia[/i]. 

In Aztec culture, coyotes were a symbol of [b]cunning [/b]and [b]worldly wisdom[/b], Huehuecoyotl is also associated with [b]worldly desires [/b]and [b]unbridled sexuality[/b]: he is one of those gods considered as a combination between good and evil.

[b]Alex Loera [/b]is the talented artist in our team who designed these versions of Huehuecoyotl.

notes.title: Tzizimine
notes.content:
The mythical world of [i]Mictlan [/i]is wide and it hides the scariest deities, so terrifying that they could not be imagined... because we've drawn them for you! 

Here we present to you the [b]Tzizimine[/b], women-like creatures, with rotten, decaying flesh which reveal the skeleton underneath, with clawed hands and feet, wearing ornaments made of [b]skull necklaces[/b] and[b] human hearts[/b].

The Tzizimine are [b]nocturnal deities[/b] whose purpose was to devour human beings at the end of the Fifth Sun. They would descend from the sky at night and stalk the little kids to kidnap them. They would also appear in the [b]eclipses [/b]to eat the sun and swallow the entire humanity.

Our visual artist [b]Sergio Vázquez Heredia[/b] has created different versions of these creatures: from [b]beautiful women[/b] who wait for travelers at the crossroads, to rotten and [b]hungry creatures[/b].

notes.title: Tlatoani
notes.content:
The [b]tlatoani [/b]was an important figure in the Aztec Empire because they essentially controlled and organized the government, military and economy of the [i]altepetl[/i], the Mesoamerica city-states.

They held the most important position in the Aztec capital of [b]Tenochtitlan[/b], in terms of political hierarchy, and were generally people from [b]higher classes[/b], descendants from[b] royal families [/b]present at that time. 

On the other hand, the leader who ruled over all of the other [i]altepetls [/i]in the Aztec Empire had the title of ‘[i]huey tlatoani[/i]’ or ‘Great Speaker’.

As you can see from the concept art of our team, Tlatoani wore [b]fine clothes[/b], jewelry, capes and emblems.

notes.title: Santiago Mataindios
notes.content:
[b]Santiago Matamoros[/b] was the patron saint of the conquest and colonization of the Americas by Spain. 

It's him that the Spanish summoned to [b]convert Indigenous people[/b] to Christianity. Santiago was also believed to have [b]miraculously helped [/b]Spanish Christians in their long struggle against the Caliphate of Cordoba, during the so-called “[b]Reconquest[/b]”.

Over the centuries, Santiago Mataindios became [b]syncretized with native deities[/b], especially those associated with water (such as Tlaloc and Chaac), to the point of becoming the patron saint of [b]rain [/b]and [b]harvest[/b].

He is an important historical character who could not be missing from our world of [i]Mictlan[/i]. 
On the basis of the[url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3046098629062626723 ] concept art we showed you a while ago[/url], our team has created a 3D model, highlighting his Hispanic [b]knight attire[/b] and his distinctly [b]Iberian features[/b], with a touch of [b]warrior majesty[/b], but at the same time a [b]serene semblance[/b], appropriate to the image of the saint.

Do you think we should [b]show [/b]Santiago Mataindios's face or keep it [b]hidden [/b]out of respect? Let us know in the comments!

notes.title: Patolli
notes.content:
We have a [b]surprise[/b] for those who are signing up to our Kickstarter campaign: exclusive access to the most popular pre-Columbian culture [b]strategy game[/b]: the [b]Patoli[/b].

Patolli was played by [b]Mesoamerican groups[/b] such as the Teotihuacans, Toltecs, Mayas and Aztecs. It was played from about 200 BCE until the arrival of the Spanish conquistadors and their conquest of the Aztec Empire in the early 1500s CE. The game was very popular across [b]all social strata[/b]: there were even matches held between the [b]rulers [/b]of neighboring villages. 

The Patoli is played on a [b]board [/b]with a diagonal-shaped cross, divided in 52 boxes that represent the Mayan calendar wheel (related to “Fuego Nuevo” – New Fire), and the “Huehuetiliztli" (104 year cycle). [b]Black beans[/b] with a hole drilled in one side were used as dice; this is why patolli is sometimes called the bean game. The [b]aim [/b]is to complete a full lap of the board with their pieces before the other player. 

The game had a strong focus on [b]gambling[/b], people would bet their precious objects, possessions and even their freedom.

Aare you curious to try this ancient game?

notes.title: Tenochtitlan
notes.content:
[b]Tenochtitlan[/b], the capital of the Aztec empire, was founded by the Aztec or Mexica people around 1325 C.E. According to [b]legend[/b], the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan after leaving their homeland of Aztlan at the direction of their god, [b]Huitzilopochtli[/b]. Huitzilopochtli instructed them to build their city in the location where they saw an[b] eagle perched on a cactus[/b] while eating a snake. 

This would be the signal that they had [b]found their home[/b].

We're bringing Tenochtitlan back to life in [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i], so that you'll enjoy its bustling heart and street life, [b]wandering[/b] around, [b]interacting [/b]with the environment and with all the [b]people [/b]inhabiting the place.

After our [b]research phase[/b] involving articles, writings, stories, codices etc. we create every spot and building planning it out with careful consideration and with a great level of detail, guided by the [b]mood board[/b] precedently created to choose the right colors, shapes and details which help us give our creations a sense of [b]authenticity[/b].

[h3]Are you excited about the idea of walking around the great capital of the Aztec civilization?

Leave us a comment![/h3]

notes.title: Xelhua
notes.content:
[b]Xelhua [/b]is a controversial mythical figure. According to the texts of Torquemada "From other opinions of how these lands were populated", Xelhua was the first son of the couple who survived the universal [b]flood[/b], Iztac Mixcuatl and Llantecuhtli. 

Xelhua was one of the seven [b]giants [/b]in Aztec mythology who escaped the flood by ascending the mountain of Tlaloc in the terrestrial paradise and afterwards built the [i]Tlachihualtepetl [/i]or pyramid of [i]Cholula[/i].

Christian chroniclers found in his figure an allusion to the mythical King Nimrod, builder of the [b]Tower of Babel[/b], and even saw in the ruins of [i]Tlachihualtepelt [/i]what remained of this mythical tower, Xelhua being associated with the arrogance of standing above the divine.

To this day there are still discrepancies about the true identity of Xelhua, whether he was a giant or if he was the founder of the city of Cholula. Nevertheless, we wanted to maintain [b]fantastic elements[/b] in his appearance, so we imagined him as a giant, with references to Tlaloc (The Rain God).

notes.title: Ñuhu
notes.content:
The [b]Mixtec[/b], the third largest group of native Mexican peoples, inhabiting the region known as La Mixteca, used the term [b]Ñuhu [/b]to refer to their [b]sacred beings[/b], also considered as protectors of crops.

Ñuhu were the [b]spirits of earth[/b] that lived in nature. They could appear in rivers, springs, roads and [b]rocks[/b]. As a matter of fact, Mixtec codex, they are represented as [b]anthropomorphic rocks[/b] decorated with red paint and small rectangular projections above their heads and around their body.

You will encounter several of these spirits during your journey in [i]Mictlan[/i]: the Ñuhu will help you unlock [b]different paths of your destiny.[/b] 

What do you think? Let us know in the comments!

notes.title: Tepoztecatl
notes.content:
The god of drunkenness and fertility, god of the copper axe, lord of [i]Tepoztlan[/i], of the mountain and its waters, makes his entrance to [i]Mictlan[/i]!

[b]Tepoztecatl [/b]was one of the four hundred Aztec gods of [b]pulque[/b], the traditional drink of the Aztecs: fermented agave (or maguey) juice.

According to the myth, Tepoztecatl was present with the other gods ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/3066366095787081604]Mayahuel[/url], Patecatl, Yauhtecatl, Totoltecatl) in the mountain [b]Chichinauhia[/b], where they prepared the legendary wine and tasted it for the first time.

The legend also depicts Tepoztecatl as a hero born from the Axitla spring and as being the one who killed the monster king Xochicalcatl, thus liberating the [b]land of Morelos[/b]. [i]El Tepozteco[/i], in the Mexican state of Morelos, is an archaeological site named after the deity.

notes.title: The creative process behind the scenes
notes.content:
Here is a [b]sneak peek [/b]behind the curtains of the development process of [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale.[/i]

There is a [b]very long process[/b] behind every scene we intend to bring on the screen when our videogame will be finally ready. First of all, the idea of how the scene should be presented is conveyed through [b]concept art[/b], then a [b]mood board[/b] is created in order to communicate the "feel" of our idea and, according to it, lightening, colors and tones are defined.

This is only the first step, followed by a long process going through blocking, 3D recreation, ambiance, post-processing, animation, cameras, dialogues, cinematics, music, sound effects... [b]Everything has to be perfect[/b] in order to create the best videogame we can create, always keeping in mind the final look and feel we want to convey in [i]Mictlan[/i].

In today's post, we are sharing with you some of the [b]sketches [/b]that our amazing concept art team has created, along with a mood board which serves as a reference in this particular scene. 

[h3]What do these images communicate to you? Let us know in the comments![/h3]

notes.title: #TributoATonantzin
notes.content:
[h3]This week we want to celebrate all the extraordinary [b]Tonantzin[/b] in our lives![/h3]

In Nahuatl, the word “[i]Nantli[/i]” means "[b]mother[/b]", so the meaning of “[i]Tonantzin[/i]” is “[b]our beloved mother[/b]”, which was how the ancient Mexicas used to call the mother goddess: [b]Coatlicue[/b]. 

We want to celebrate all the women that have raised, educated and accompanied us in our lives. It doesn't matter if they are your biological mothers or not, your sisters, your mentors or your friends.

notes.title: Mayahuel
notes.content:
[b]Mayahuel [/b] is the central Mexican goddess of the [b]maguey plant[/b], the female deity also associated with fertility, fecundity and nourishment.

According to the legend, one night, Quetzalcoatl went to the godess and convinced her to descend on Earth with him. Once on Earth, they [b]bound themselves into a tree[/b] to flee from the evil Tzintzinmitl. 

Tzintzinmitl found out about what the two had done and destroyed the branch of the tree where Mayahuel was, [b]striking her dead[/b]. Quetzalcoatl buried the remains of his beloved in a nearby field. From her remains, later on, emerged a[b] beautiful plant[/b] from which, when its trunk it's scraped, a [b]sweet liquid[/b] flows.

When fermented, the liquid becomes [i]pulque[/i], the[b] liquid of the gods[/b]. Pulque was used in Aztec rituals and ceremonies, as well as in celebrations and festivals, and is still enjoyed today by contemporary Mexicans. 

[i]Have you ever tried it[/i]?

notes.title: Xochipilli
notes.content:
In one of our [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2992053531614891693]previous updates[/url], we showed you the concept art of [b]Xochipilli[/b], the "flower prince", the God of dance, music, arts, drunkenness, carnal love and, in his [i]Macuilxochitl [/i](5 flower) form, the patron of the game [i]patolli[/i]. You can read more about this fascinating character [url=https://steamcommunity.com/games/1411900/announcements/detail/2992053531614891693]here[/url]!

Today we're showing you the latest render of Xochipilli. He truly is a flamboyant deity with an uninhibited character, the life of the party in [i]Mictlan[/i]! 

We decided to model an [b]androgynous face[/b] due to the feminine and masculine energy he emanates, like many other young and beautiful gods in prehispanic iconography.

Our Xochipilli wears a nose accessory made of jade (the one in codex Borgia) and a bezote described by Sahagun's informants. His hair is blond like the solar gods' hair and he wears a headdress inspired by the quetzal band in codex Laúd.  

Fray Bernardino's informants also described his facial paint as "simulating tears". We reinterpreted this as [b]golden néctar tears[/b].

What do you think about this character? Do you like our model so far? We'd like to hear your voice!

notes.title: Omecuaime
notes.content:
In many prehispanic and colonial codices, are written stories about the [b]fall of the Great Tenochtitlan[/b]. 
[b]Apocalyptic scenes[/b] emerge from the texts, which describe "signals in the sky": comets, sun eclipse and also, walking the very earth, the sight of [b]monsters[/b].

In Nahual mythology, one of the most terrible creatures was the [b]Omecuaime[/b], also known as [b]Tlacanetzolli[/b]. The horrendous beast with an ashen-skinned body had two heads and four massive arms: a creepy creature releasing an [b]unbearable stink[/b] that would [b]literally suffocate[/b] the victim. 

Anyone coming across a Omecuaime would perish under its [b]mortal hug[/b]: the monster would extract their [b]Tonalli [/b]([b]soul[/b]), squeezing it out of the victim's body, regardless of who he or she was: a merchant, a soldier, a powerful warrior, and even a monarch.

These mythical and deadly creatures will be part of the [b]perilous world [/b]of [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i]... so if you see them from afar, you better[b] run for your life[/b].

notes.title: Ixpuxtequi
notes.content:
In Mexica mythology, [b]Ixpuxtequi [/b]is a terrible monster that wanders into the night, hunting defenseless, lonely travelers on the road. Its name in Nahua means "[b]broken face[/b]", as this creature appears as a humanoid figure, with long, eagle legs and [b]without the lower jaw[/b]. 

It carries a long staff to lean on, its [b]menacing figure[/b] hunting the living beings and their nightmares. Seeing it, meant certain doom.
Considered one of the four deities of death, Ixpuxtequi brings bad luck and misfortunes. Its wife is the goddess of fear and horror, [b]Nexoxco[/b].

notes.title: Quinametzin
notes.content:
The [b]Quinametzin [/b] are the race of giants that inhabited Mexico in ancient times.

We are working on five different versions of these [b]mythical giants[/b], experimenting with various designs, very different from the first versions that we presented to you when we first started the development of [i]Mictlan[/i].

There are many [b]stories and myths[/b] in Mesoamerican cultures about these mythical creatures, So far, we have included in our game [b]three different versions[/b] of these giants, and we are also working on different types of mechanics and various body types: elongated Mayan skulls, tree-like creatures, giant orcs...

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/06096094bf6dc7e9b5cba89098ce5277f2f92b42.jpg[/img]

There are so many [b]Mesoamerican myths[/b] that it is almost impossible for us to cover all of them in our game. Moreover, we're hoping that, in time, we [b]will be raising more funds[/b] to help our development process, so that we are able to integrate more characters, beasts, and all kinds of creatures from the Mesoamerican folklore in [i]Mictlan[/i]. 

Remember that [i]Mictlan [/i] is an indie project, we need your support to continue with this laborious and expensive process, your help is invaluable to us!

notes.title: Mercenaries
notes.content:
[b]Mercenaries [/b]joined the Conquest and raced to capture the wealth of the New World.

They came from Spain in search of adventures, new life opportunities, personal ambition but, most of all, [b]looking for a quick fortune[/b].
Indigenous communities were attacked and enslaved and any [b]treasures [/b]they may have had (such as gold, silver or pearls) were taken from them.

Most of these men, with few if any morals and/or education, were responsible for [b]cruel crimes[/b] and killings, willing to do anything to get what they wanted.

Mercenaries wore a [b]great variety of clothes[/b]: pants, shirts, jackets or simple leather jerkins. They wore no uniform because they didn't identify with any military group.

notes.title: War Dogs
notes.content:
[b]Dogs [/b]have always been [b]men's best friends[/b]. Men originally domesticated dogs by adopting cubs into their tribes and feeding them. Since then, not only dogs became their faithful companions, but they also had an important role in [b]wars[/b].

As a matter of fact, dogs in warfare have a very long history starting in [b]ancient times[/b]. Those adorable little puppies would be trained to sink their long, sharp teeth into the flesh of the enemies.

The use of war dogs goes back to the time of Greeks, Persians, Egyptians, Britons and Romans. These civilizations all used dogs in battles, often sending them into battle with [b]spiked collars and coats of mail armour[/b]. Attila the Hun used giant Molosser dogs (similar to the mastiff) in his military campaigns.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/3634136006a71ff900cf2de84422a3dc88675275.jpg[/img]

[b]Mastiffs [/b]and other large breeds were used by the Spanish conquistadors against native Americans in the 1500s. Indigenous peoples, who were used to small dog breeds of docile nature, suffered greatly, both physically and mentally, from the attacks by these[b] large and aggressive animals[/b] during battles. 

When they first met the Spanish war dogs, indigenous people even thought that those might be [b]some species of dragon[/b] - an impression derived from the fact that Spanish war dogs were armored in chainmail and steel plate, like their masters.

One of the [b]bloodiest punishments[/b] used during the Conquest was the [b][i]aperreamiento[/i][/b]: the defenseless victim, because of an act of rebellion or the practice of sodomy, was brutally attacked and killed by a [b]pack of hungry, trained dogs[/b].

notes.title: The Patron of All
notes.content:
[h3]Are you wondering who this mysterious, hooded, spectral-looking man is...?[/h3]

He is none other than the [b]apostle Santiago[/b], whose apparitions during the time of the conquest, riding a splendid white horse, astonished all of those who were present. 

Santiago is identified as the [b]patron saint of the conquest[/b] since the Spanish army entrusted their victory to him. 

In ancient writings are recorded [b]Santiago's apparitions[/b], depicting him in shining armor, wielding a sword, with a flowing cloak around his shoulders.

The saint has also a great significance among Mexican people and in a great part of Latin America, it is said that he appeared in Mexico, during the conquest, in the following sites: 

- Centla, currently Tabasco State in 1519; 
- Pedro de Alvarado in Tenochtitlán in 1520; 
- To the troops of Nuño de Guzman, during the the Battle of Tetlán, Jalisco, in 1530; 
- Querétaro, during the conquest of the Chichimecas.

Long after the conquest, he went from being the apostle of the conquerors to being the apostle of the indigenous,[b] patron saint of rain and harvest[/b].

notes.content:
According to the different traditions of Mesoamerican cultures, it is believed that the first creature to cross over the ashes spread before a newborn baby becomes that child’s [b]nahual[/b], a [b]guardian spirit[/b]. 

Every newborn has their own personal guardian, depending on their day of birth. A spirit that watches over them and [b]protects them[/b]. 

Kids can acquire [b]gifts [/b]and [b]special powers[/b] from their nahual, which can take the form of [b]various animals[/b] such as a jaguar, an eagle, a deer, or a snake (among others).

In this [b]concept art [/b]from our talented team of artists, you can see some of the [b]younger characters [/b]you will encounter in [i]Mictlan[/i], each one with their own characteristics, skills and magic powers, each of them with challanges to overcome and adventurres to live!

notes.title: Macuilcuetzpalin
notes.content:
In the Mexica pantheon, there are five Gods who are the embodiment of excess, overindulgence, pleasure and drunkenness. 
They are known as [b]Ahuiateteo [/b], "Gods of pleasure" or as [b]Macuiltonaleque [/b]"Spirits of days 5", (because all their calendrical names start with this number).
 
Today we're showing you the concept art of [b]Macuilcuetzpalin [/b](5 Lizard), the [b]God of pleasure[/b], whose body is painted in black ink. Designed by our concept artist [b]Josue Diaz[/b] with the features of our very own Creative Director and founder [b]Guillermo Alarcon[/b]. 

Macuilcuetzpalin is characterized for his [b]warrior-like attributes[/b], being the only one out of the five Gods wielding darts and a distinctive shield ([i]chimalli[/i]). 

Would you like to meet all of the five Gods of excess? 
Would you rather [b]fight [/b]them or have them as your [b]ally[/b]?

notes.title: Tzompantli
notes.content:
The sight of a [b]sea of skulls[/b] pierced by spears and displayed in front of the temples is one of the frequent images in the codices of many [b]Mesoamerican civilizations[/b] such as the Mexica, Maya, and Toltec.

The [b]cult of death[/b] that pervades our country sinks its roots into a world where the cycle of [b]life-sacrifice-death[/b] becomes a natural process and where there is an acceptance of the [b]short-lived existence [/b]of beings and things, and where the upholding existence of the cosmos, the world and men, depends on [b]sacrifices to the Gods[/b], which in return offer their protection.

In [i]Mictlan [/i]we will honor this worldview inherited by our [b]ancestors[/b].

[u][b]Note[/b][/u]: This is just a [b]WIP[/b], it doesn't represent the finalized version of our game title, and the end result will be most likely completely different.

notes.title: The Jaguar Warrior
notes.content:
We are very proud to show you the rendered version of a [b]Jaguar[/b] ([i]ocelotl[/i]) Warrior, who will appear in the game as NPC.

Jaguar Warriors were members of the [b]Aztec military elite[/b]. They had to prove their value and courage on the battlefield by capturing [b]prisoners [/b]and [b]fighting valiantly[/b]. Only then, they could wear the [b]jaguar's tlahuiztli [/b](uniform), a jaguar motif which was associated to [b]Tezcatlipoca [/b]and was also believed to give the warriors the animal's strengths during battles. 

The NPC you see in the video (a [b]work-in-progress[/b]) was knighted "jaguar" by [b]Ahuitzotzin [/b]for his distinguished service in the [b]Tzicoac campaign[/b]. Since then, he participated in many wars, bearing the marks of his battles on his [i]tlahuiztli[/i]. 
The pelt is torn showing his [i]ichcahuipilli [/i]underneath, a leather band is tied around his knee after suffering from a severe injury and, in a fierce battle, his [i]cuatepoztli [/i](helmet) was split open due to a powerful strike. 

For this Jaguar Warrior, every mark, every scar is an [b]emblem of pride[/b], that's why he decided to display them boastfully on his uniform... maybe it's also possible that, with the old age, he's become[b] a bit sentimental[/b]...?

[h3]What do you think? Let us know in the comments![/h3]

notes.title: The Wetlands
notes.content:
Greetings to our [i]Mictlan[/i]'s community!

Today we want to show you one of the [b]biomes [/b]that will be a part of our open world: the [b]wetlands[/b]. 

Mesoamerica is a region abundant in wetlands such as swamps, marshlands and estuarios. These territories with a [b]rich biodiversity[/b] were widely exploited since the arrival of the first nomadic human populations to the continent, with activities like fishing, hunting and gathering of both plants and shellfish. 

The important role this ecosystem played in the[b] development of prehispanic culture[/b] inspired us to recreate this kind of location so that the players may experience the [b]beauty [/b]and the [b]uniqueness [/b]of this environment. 

These screenshots are [b]real-time renders [/b]from our open world, without RTX Ray Tracing. This is what the scenarios will look like in old computer systems and consoles such as the PS4. 

In a couple of months, we will present a [b]technical demo [/b]with our RTX Ray Tracing environments to all of you who want to play [i]Mictlan [/i]on a high-end gaming machine or on the [b]latest generation consoles[/b] such as the Playstation 5.

notes.title: Xochipilli
notes.content:
[b]Xochipilli[/b], the "flower prince" in Nahuatl, is the God of dance, music, arts, drunkenness, carnal love and, in his [i]Macuilxochitl [/i](5 flower) form, the patron of the game [i]patolli[/i]. 

Everyone in ancient Mexico had a God who protected and guided them, in exchange for sacrificial offerings. Xochipilli, in particular, is a God closely tied to [b]sexuality[/b], [b]homosexuality [/b]and [b]bisexuality[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/4f5d8c288bee6465f2af9bb0f5db23d73340caca.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/b87400066b0d81a547a88d39ad46c25a9809848f.jpg[/img]

[b]Sahagún [/b]describes him with a [b]floral headdress[/b], which reflects his role as patron of music and songs, his body lightly painted in [b]red[/b], his figure adorned with [b]jade[/b], [b]turquoise [/b]and [b]mother-of-pearl[/b]. 

[b]His statue[/b], which was unearthed on the side of the volcano [i]Popocatépetl [/i]near [i]Tlalmanalco[/i], is decorated with carvings of different type of [b]flowers[/b], such as the [i]ololiuhqui [/i]and the tobacco flower, as well as [i]teonanácatl[/i], also known as the [b]Flesh of the Gods[/b], which is a psychotropic mushroom usually eaten during the festivities and sacrifice, inducing an [b]altered state of consciousness[/b] in their users.

As a matter of fact, his[b] trance-like face[/b] carved in the statue has been interpreted as being in a state of [b]spiritual ecstasy[/b].

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/7daa71bb3218a02a7a3f89a66602951d5ae08ac3.jpg[/img]
[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/72b88dc2559bc2cf095fa8092c0e60ffd5a191a6.jpg[/img]

[h3]Xochipilli is certainly another mystical and important figure joining our [b]pantheon of Gods[/b] you'll be seeing in [i]Mictlan[/i] (have you checked out [url=https://store.steampowered.com/news/app/1411900/view/3025824821129123543]Tezcatlipoca: God of the Night Sky[/url]?)[/h3]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/38746200/e5afd894e9c2f73e89e98172f3a6a299439979d7.jpg[/img]

Let us know in the comments what you think! [/h3]

notes.title: Spanish soldiers: a concept art
notes.content:
Today we're showing you the concept art of what [b]Spanish conquistadores[/b] will look like in [i]Mictlan[/i].

As you can see from the picture by our talented artist [b]Josue Diaz[/b], Spanish soldiers wore heavy and gleaming armor, with robes under a huge, metal breastplate.

As their armors deteriorated in time, during the period of the Conquest, they started[b] replacing some parts[/b] with different elements from the area, more suitable to the local atmospheric and natural conditions, and also more suitable for [b]battles [/b]and [b]survival in the New World[/b]. The same happened with their [b]weapons[/b], as Spanish soldiers in many cases replaced the ones they brought from their country with the typical weapons used by [b]Mexica warriors[/b].

[h3]Did you know that, in one of Mictlan's campaigns, you'll be able to [b]play as a Spanish general[/b] during the first years of the Conquest?[/h3]

notes.title: The road so far...
notes.content:
It might sound corny, but you have no idea how [b]blessed [/b]and [b]proud [/b]I feel to have embarked on this amazing journey to create [i]Mictlan: An Ancient Mythical Tale[/i]. 

Recreating part of our [b]history[/b], celebrating [b]ancestral cultures[/b], reviving thousand-year-old [b]tales [/b]in a video game, it is truly a dream come true, something I've been fantasizing about since childhood. 

Many years later, I find myself [b]living the dream[/b], working with a talented team of archaeologists, anthropologists, concept artists, 3D designers and my marketing team, all of us riding on this train, moving along, reaching [i]Mictlan[/i].

We have been working for months [b]without rest[/b]. We are tired, but we love what we're doing. The need, the love, the aspiration to create the first open-world video game revolving around the [b]Mesoamerican culture[/b] and the ancient people of Mexico, is the gasoline that keeps us going everyday, encouraging us to pour everything we have in this project.

I would like to [b]thank [/b]my amazing [i]Mictlan [/i]team, without them I would not have been able to get to where we are. We have achieved so much in so little time, but still,[b] the road is long [/b]and we still have another 2 or 3 years of development to go. I'm sure that tears will be shed, tears of frustration and happiness, but it will all be[b] worth it[/b]. 

We believe in [i]Mictlan [/i]and I want to personally thank[b] all of you,[/b] in our [b]community[/b], who have been following us since the beginning. We're not just a community anymore, we've become a [b]family [/b]which is continuing to expand. We are inspired and have inspired other developers as well, changing, in a way, the ecosystem of the video game industry. 

I can't wait to see what else awaits us, but [b]we'll find out together[/b]! 

Once again a sincere thank you, to all of you, the [i]Mictlan [/i]team, our ancestors, and the legacy that our grandparents left us.

Sincerely,

[i][b]Guillermo Alarcon[/b][/i]
Creative Director Mictlan

notes.title: The great market of Tlatelolco
notes.content:
The [b]great market of Tlatelolco[/b] was one of the largest commercial exchange centers of ancient Mexico before the European conquest. It was founded alongside the city of Tlatelolco in the [b]year 1337[/b], and for a time it rivaled its neighbor and twin city, [b]Tenochtitlan[/b], until it was conquered by Mexica Tlatoani Axayacatl in the year 1473. 

Since then, it became a very important [b]commercial center[/b], where people from the basin of the Valley of Mexico traded intensely, and merchants arrived continuously from [b]all corners of Mesoamerica[/b] to exchange their products. 

The level of [b]organization [/b]and [b]variety of products[/b] was such that it astonished the Spanish conquerors.

[b]Hernán Cortés[/b], in one of his letters, wrote about the market: 
[h3][i]
This city has many public squares where there is continuous trading, buying and selling. There is another square – twice as big the city of Salamanca – even surrounded by portals, where every day there are over sixty thousand souls buying and selling….[/i][/h3]

Take a look at the concept art by [b]Josue Diaz[/b], a talented artist from our team, of the great market of Tlatelolco which we are recreating in [i]Mictlan[/i], bringing to life this key location for exchanging goods in ancient Mexica civilization.

notes.title: Amoxoaque
notes.content:
The [b]Amoxoaque[/b] were [b]great sages[/b] who, since ancient times, used to make their rituals in the sacred city of Teotihuacan. It is said that the Amoxoaque came to our land during the [b]dark times[/b]. They arrived by boat to Panoayan and, from there, started a[b] long pilgrimage[/b] to Tamoanchan, near Teotihuacan, where they finally settled down. 

Today, only [b]four sages [/b]remain among us: Oxomoco, Cipactonal, Tlaltetequi and Xochicauaca, who knew the art of [b]reading the stars[/b] and [b]dreams[/b]. 
 
The recent oral tradition depicts these ancient creatures as [b]tree people [/b]who protect [b]forests [/b]and [b]jungles[/b], that's why our concept art team decided to focus on this element to represent the Amoxoaque. 

Take a look at the stunning work by [b]Jorge H Flores[/b], who managed to combine history and fantasy, bringing these [b]colossal creatures[/b] to life. On their rough bark-like skin you can also see the ancestral engravings from the [b]Cascajal slate[/b], one of the oldest writing expressions in Mesoamerica.
